高盛美国经济学家Pierfrancesco Mei将当前美国经济定性为具有韧性，并预计在基准情景下——美联储12月再加息一次，随后于2027年下半年启动三次降息，10年期美债收益率年底降至4.4%——高利率对2027年GDP增长的拖累仅约0.2个百分点。
然而，若收益率维持在当前水平，拖累效应将超过0.5个百分点。从传导渠道看，30年期抵押贷款利率突破7%，将进一步压制住宅投资；消费支出将因耐用品需求走弱受到约0.2个百分点的拖累；而非AI企业在债务到期再融资过程中利息支出的上升，预计将令资本开支增长承压约0.3个百分点。
高盛全球经济学家Joseph Briggs与Johan Allen则构建了量化规则框架：每100个基点的利率上行，将使主要发达经济体住宅投资下降约6%，消费者支出平均下降约0.2%，企业资本开支下降约1.8%，合计对发达经济体GDP产生约0.6个百分点的拖累。在财政层面，大额基本赤字叠加高利率，预计将推动美国债务占GDP比率在2035年升至124%（基准情景）乃至132%（若当前利率持续）。
经济是否真的"韧性"？Zandi提出异见
在整体基调相对偏乐观的市场讨论中，Mark Zandi是立场最为谨慎的声音。他认为，用"韧性"描述美国经济"令人着迷，近乎令人沮丧"，正确的描述应该是"脆弱"。
Zandi指出，劳动力市场是最清晰的疲软信号。过去一年月均新增就业约4万人，剔除医疗行业后几近为零；失业率虽仍低，但部分归因于劳动参与率下降，若加以调整，实际失业率将处于4%中段水平，高于充分就业水平。实际工资增长对于中低收入群体而言实际上是负增长，家庭储蓄正被持续消耗。
在总量数据上，Zandi对约2%的实际GDP增长率并不感到安慰。他估计其中约三分之一，即0.6至0.7个百分点，来自AI相关活动（包括AI资本开支净贡献及AI相关股价财富效应）。这意味着非AI经济体的增长率仅约1%至1.5%，"是一个相当糟糕的经济状态"。
Zandi还将美国财政状况描述为"我所见过的最糟糕的情形"：赤字超过GDP的6%，基本赤字超过3%，债务约为GDP的100%且预计10年后将升至125%，联邦利息支出已超过1万亿美元并将快速上升。他给出的风险概率判断是：严重债券市场抛售的概率约为四分之一，经济彻底脱轨的概率约为三分之一。
银行与信用市场：尚在可控范围
尽管Mark Zandi对金融系统潜在断裂风险保持高度警惕，高盛分析师对银行及信用市场的判断相对温和。
IMF前货币与资本市场部门主任Tobias Adrian与高盛金融股票研究组主管Richard Ramsden均认为银行无需过度担忧。Ramsden指出，鉴于美国银行资产敏感型资产负债结构，利率上行应有助于提升净利息收入；在不出现更广泛经济下行的前提下，信用质量亦不会出现显著恶化；在计提利率驱动的证券组合浮亏后，大多数银行仍应保有超额资本。
在信用市场，高盛首席信用策略师Amanda Lynam认为，高利率对企业信用的冲击在当前稳健增长背景下总体可控，不足以引发违约率显著上升。但她也指出，若利率波动率重回2022至2023年的高位，依赖收益率驱动的机构投资者信心将受到冲击，届时对投资级信用市场的需求将面临实质性压力。
美股：当前利率尚不构成威胁，但上行风险不可忽视
高盛首席美国股票策略师Ben Snider认为，当前收益率水平不应阻止美股继续走高。尽管今年以来标普500指数市盈率从23倍降至19倍，但强劲的盈利增长（过去12个月增速超30%）已足以抵消估值压缩的影响，且目前股债相对估值——以标普500盈利收益率与10年期实际美债收益率之差衡量——约为230个基点，过去两年保持相对稳定，显示估值已基本完成对高收益率的再校准。

然而，Snider同时提出两个需密切关注的风险点：其一，若10年期美债收益率在单月内上行超过约50个基点（即两个标准差），将触发美股历史上的典型承压模式；其二，小市值股、房地产及住宅建筑商等利率敏感板块已出现明显分化，市场广度已降至互联网泡沫以来最低水平。高盛多资产策略师Christian Mueller-Glissmann与Andrea Ferrario补充指出，更高的债券收益率正在强化债券在多资产组合中的战略配置价值，最优债券配置比例应向35%至55%的长期均值靠拢，但目前强劲的盈利增长仍令股票相对债券更具吸引力。
AI：高增长叙事下的潜在最脆弱环节
在当前的经济与市场讨论中，AI既是支撑增长的核心引擎，也是高利率环境下最受关注的潜在脆弱点。

从乐观角度看，高盛分析认为AI资本开支承压风险有限。超大规模云计算企业（Hyperscalers）的资本开支迄今对高利率和成本上升表现出强劲韧性，构成美国AI投资的逾三分之二；MSFT、META、AMZN、GOOGL、NVDA等主要AI相关发行主体信用评级普遍在AAA至AA级，AAA/AA级别发行主体的利息覆盖倍数高达27.7倍，净杠杆仅0.5倍，具备充裕的债务容纳空间；Lynam也认为，AI相关债务发行被颠覆的门槛极高。
然而，Tobias Adrian对AI复合体中的三重风险表示关注：多家AI企业之间的投资互联性与循环性，意味着一家企业的盈利冲击可能迅速扩散；AI企业与投资者通过杠杆ETF和衍生品形成的杠杆叠加杠杆的结构；以及AI企业的强劲营收增长能否持续这一根本性不确定性。
Mark Zandi的警告则最为直接："如果利率在当前水平或更高水平再持续一两个季度，AI可能成为经济中首先断裂的那一环。"他指出，持续的高利率将压制AI相关股价，财富效应的逆转将进一步打压消费，而融资成本上升将使维持当前AI建设速度所需资本的筹集愈加困难。目前，AI在很大程度上依靠其自身的动能与市场乐观情绪运行，但这一状态的持续时间存在高度不确定性。

items.title: 美银警告AI泡沫破裂信号：美股与美债收益率同步下跌
items.summary:
美国银行衍生品团队发出警告，当AI泡沫最终破裂时，市场将呈现与过去数月截然不同的走势——不是"股跌债跌"（即股票下跌、美债收益率上升），而是股票与收益率同步下行。


10月8日，英国《金融时报》披露OpenAI年化收入远低于市场流传数字，当日纳斯达克指数重挫逾1%，费城半导体指数跌3.4%，而美债收益率也随即走低——
items.text:
美国银行衍生品团队发出警告，当AI泡沫最终破裂时，市场将呈现与过去数月截然不同的走势——不是"股跌债跌"（即股票下跌、美债收益率上升），而是股票与收益率同步下行。


10月8日，英国《金融时报》披露OpenAI年化收入远低于市场流传数字，当日纳斯达克指数重挫逾1%，费城半导体指数跌3.4%，而美债收益率也随即走低——债券市场表现出罕见的避险属性。美国银行衍生品团队在最新一期《全球股票波动率洞察》报告中将这次单日闪崩定性为"AI解仓的最佳预演"，并指出更关键的信号在于：彼时美债收益率与股市同步下行，而非出现市场几个月来已习以为常的"股跌债涨"格局。


这一模式随即在10月14日得到复制。当日美国CPI通胀数据超预期，10年期美债收益率一度飙升，加息预期概率短暂突破50%，但随着云计算基础设施企业CoreWeave股价崩跌逾15%、信用违约互换利差扩大135个基点，债市收益率涨势迅速逆转，收益率最终接近持平收盘。


15日，10年期美债收益率继续大幅下行10个基点至5.09%，触及三周低点。与此同时，MSCI亚太股票指数重挫逾3%，韩国综合指数单日一度暴跌9%，三星、SK海力士跌幅一度达到两位数。标普500期货跌0.4%，纳斯达克100期货跌逾1%。

美国银行认为，这正是AI泡沫破裂的"传导链条"：私人AI生态的压力最先、最猛烈地冲击纳斯达克，同时将债市拉向避险模式。


AI特有的风险冲击，纳斯达克首当其冲

美国银行股票挂钩团队Benjamin Bowler、Nitin Saksena、Arjun Goyal等人指出，10月8日纳斯达克对大盘的大幅跑输，与过去数年每一次AI特定风险事件的表现高度吻合——从2025年1月的DeepSeek冲击，到今年夏天的半导体板块回调，规律如出一辙。

报告认为，这反映了纳斯达克对"私人AI生态"的高敝口。OpenAI、Anthropic等私人AI公司一旦出现裂缝，纳斯达克100指数即为公开市场中首先承压的代理标的。该行将其定为AI交易——无论多空——的首选指数。


这一传导路径正面临新的压力测试。Anthropic于10月14日向华尔街开放财务数据，而OpenAI 200亿美元的"总收入与净收入缺口"仍悬而未决，私人端向公开市场的传导渠道料将持续受到考验。

债市异动：两次AI冲击均触发收益率同步下行

更值得关注的是债市的行为模式。过去数月，美股与美债收益率持续呈现反向关系，债券作为对冲工具的功能几乎失效。然而，10月8日与10月14日的两次AI风险事件均打破这一格局，收益率随股市同步走低。


美国银行将其归结为AI放缓的宏观逻辑：除传统避险资金流入外，AI投资周期降温意味着资本开支减少、电力及资源消耗下降，叠加对经济增长与通胀的双重压制，将对债券形成额外利好。换言之，若AI泡沫真正破裂，债券将重新发挥对冲功能。

报告援引的历史参照是2000年互联网泡沫破裂：彼时纳斯达克100指数崩盘，10年期美债收益率从约6.5%跌至4%中段。美国银行承认两个数据点尚不构成完整规律，但认为历史先例与宏观逻辑相互印证，已足以为投资者提供结构性参考。


CoreWeave引爆信用端危机，AI股本周跑输大盘840基点

10月14日的市场抛售揭示了AI泡沫另一潜在破裂路径：信用端。


CoreWeave（CRWV）是此次风暴中心。在其2032年到期债券G-spread突破1000个基点、收益率升至15%之后，股价随之崩跌逾15%，创上市以来第三大单日跌幅。D.A. Davidson分析师Gil Luria将CoreWeave定性为AI领域的"次级抵押贷款分级"，并警告若公司无法偿付债务，股价将归零——其融资成本约为9%，而投资回报率仅约1%。CoreWeave的信用违约互换利差当日扩大135个基点，市场目前隐含的五年内违约概率已达63%。

恐慌迅速蔓延。DigitalOcean（DOCN）下跌14%，Hut 8（HUT）跌10%，Nebius（NBIS）与IREN各跌约9%；Oracle（ORCL）下挫9%，与其信用违约互换点位的背离仍未弥合。市场研究机构Gartner随即发出警告，预计80%的新兴云计算企业将在2030年前停止独立运营。


本周，AI板块相对标普500非AI成分股的累计跑输幅度已达840个基点。BTIG策略师Jonathan Krinsky同样认为，当前的痛苦交易指向"利率下行、纳斯达克下行"，若"七巨头"也开始像半导体股那样随利率同步下跌，将进一步印证其"红色十月"判断。

美银推荐对冲组合：让债市补贴期权成本

面对这一潜在风险，美国银行衍生品团队提出了一套"以债补股"的对冲结构。


传统AI泡沫对冲的难点在于时机：过早买入看跌期权，市场持续走高将不断让行权价落后于市场。美国银行的解决方案是"最大回望看跌期权"（max lookback put）——其行权价随市场上涨而持续上移，但这一特性本身成本较高。该行的创新之处在于，将期权设定为在10年期SOFR低于当前远期利率25个基点时方才生效，以此将利率下行预期转化为期权费补贴。


具体交易方案为：买入纳斯达克100指数2027年9月到期、行权价为当前价格90%的每日观测最大回望看跌期权，附加利率触发条款，指示性期权费为3.62%，较纯回望看跌期权折价46%，亦低于普通看跌期权23个基点。


回测数据显示，对该结构进行过去30年的模拟定价，其触发概率为13%（普通90%看跌期权为11%），平均价内赔付倍数为7.2倍（普通看跌期权6.1倍，纯回望期权3.9倍），最大超额收益出现于互联网泡沫破裂期间。

该结构的主要风险在于2022年式的"股跌债涨"情景，即通胀冲击或美联储意外紧缩导致股债同向下跌的格局——这恰恰是2026年大部分时间债市的运行方式，并非真正的尾部风险。


此外，美国银行同步推荐一笔VIX看涨价差交易：买入VIX 11月到期19-24点价差，指示性成本0.63美元，最大赔付倍数约7.9倍，适用于对中期选举前后波动率温和抬升的判断。

泡沫程度几何：指标显示集中于局部而非全面

美国银行泡沫风险指标（BRI）的最新读数提供了更为细化的视角。标普500指数中目前仅有13只股票BRI超过0.8，合计占指数权重约2.4%；相比之下，互联网泡沫高峰期曾有50至100只股票触及该阈值，占指数权重20%至40%。

当前泡沫特征呈现出明显的集中性：单股层面，Moderna（MRNA）、CrowdStrike（CRWD）、惠普企业（HPE）、Zebra Technologies、Revvity及Palo Alto Networks（PANW）读数靠前；板块层面，美国银行旗下美国网络安全及巴西大选主题篮子BRI均达到0.92的高位。


值得注意的是，价格层面的泡沫指标显示风险仍属局部，但Jefferies已将当前局面定性为"AI的2008时刻"，并指出两家现金消耗型AI实验室合计占据2.3万亿美元订单积压的一半。这意味着真正的泡沫风险或并不体现在股价层面，而潜伏于资产负债表之中。

波动率被人为压制，一旦松动或触发急剧反弹

表面平静之下，市场结构已暗流涌动。标普500指数5日盘中已实现波动率仅为7.6%，处于过去一年的第三百分位。但美国银行认为，这种平静是被期权做市商手中庞大的gamma敞口人为维持的。


截至10月9日，标普500对冲型gamma读数为145亿美元，为过去一年第四高。大量0DTE/1DTE期权卖出流、衍生品收益基金的结构性波动率供给共同形成了市场的"防护栏"，将盘中波动控制在极窄区间。


然而，这一缓冲正在松动。据彭博宏观策略师Michael Ball指出，标普500已跌破7775至7750点的第一道支撑位；SpotGamma将"波动率触发点"定于7775点——低于此水平，做市商的对冲行为将不再起到平抑波动的作用。一旦指数跌破7700点附近，正向gamma将急剧稀薄，逢低买入的均值回归策略或将让位于"越跌越卖"模式。

与此同时，客户已悄然大量买入VIX看涨期权，仓位水平已接近2024年夏季高点——彼时曾引发剧烈波动。这一前瞻性波动率需求使标普500期限结构异常陡峭，1个月与1周平值隐含波动率之比处于过去一年的第95百分位。


美国银行估算，若前月VIX期货出现10点跳升，做市商为维持delta中性将被迫买入相当于约90%日均VIX期货成交量的头寸，为过去一年最高读数。高盛近期亦独立得出类似结论，认为VIX触及25点的概率高于标普500下跌2%的概率。两家银行不约而同地指向同一结论：一旦波动率松动，市场反应的烈度可能远超价格本身的跌幅。


后续关注节点：今日PPI数据、Anthropic财务披露，以及本月晚些时候的大型科技公司财报季，将对上述逻辑形成直接压力测试。若标普500无法收复7750点，做市商的gamma护盾将不复存在。

blocks.x: 美国银行衍生品团队发出警告，当AI泡沫最终破裂时，市场将呈现与过去数月截然不同的走势——不是"股跌债跌"（即股票下跌、美债收益率上升），而是股票与收益率同步下行。
10月8日，英国《金融时报》披露OpenAI年化收入远低于市场流传数字，当日纳斯达克指数重挫逾1%，费城半导体指数跌3.4%，而美债收益率也随即走低——债券市场表现出罕见的避险属性。美国银行衍生品团队在最新一期《全球股票波动率洞察》报告中将这次单日闪崩定性为"AI解仓的最佳预演"，并指出更关键的信号在于：彼时美债收益率与股市同步下行，而非出现市场几个月来已习以为常的"股跌债涨"格局。
这一模式随即在10月14日得到复制。当日美国CPI通胀数据超预期，10年期美债收益率一度飙升，加息预期概率短暂突破50%，但随着云计算基础设施企业CoreWeave股价崩跌逾15%、信用违约互换利差扩大135个基点，债市收益率涨势迅速逆转，收益率最终接近持平收盘。
15日，10年期美债收益率继续大幅下行10个基点至5.09%，触及三周低点。与此同时，MSCI亚太股票指数重挫逾3%，韩国综合指数单日一度暴跌9%，三星、SK海力士跌幅一度达到两位数。标普500期货跌0.4%，纳斯达克100期货跌逾1%。
美国银行认为，这正是AI泡沫破裂的"传导链条"：私人AI生态的压力最先、最猛烈地冲击纳斯达克，同时将债市拉向避险模式。
AI特有的风险冲击，纳斯达克首当其冲
美国银行股票挂钩团队Benjamin Bowler、Nitin Saksena、Arjun Goyal等人指出，10月8日纳斯达克对大盘的大幅跑输，与过去数年每一次AI特定风险事件的表现高度吻合——从2025年1月的DeepSeek冲击，到今年夏天的半导体板块回调，规律如出一辙。
报告认为，这反映了纳斯达克对"私人AI生态"的高敝口。OpenAI、Anthropic等私人AI公司一旦出现裂缝，纳斯达克100指数即为公开市场中首先承压的代理标的。该行将其定为AI交易——无论多空——的首选指数。
这一传导路径正面临新的压力测试。Anthropic于10月14日向华尔街开放财务数据，而OpenAI 200亿美元的"总收入与净收入缺口"仍悬而未决，私人端向公开市场的传导渠道料将持续受到考验。
债市异动：两次AI冲击均触发收益率同步下行
更值得关注的是债市的行为模式。过去数月，美股与美债收益率持续呈现反向关系，债券作为对冲工具的功能几乎失效。然而，10月8日与10月14日的两次AI风险事件均打破这一格局，收益率随股市同步走低。
美国银行将其归结为AI放缓的宏观逻辑：除传统避险资金流入外，AI投资周期降温意味着资本开支减少、电力及资源消耗下降，叠加对经济增长与通胀的双重压制，将对债券形成额外利好。换言之，若AI泡沫真正破裂，债券将重新发挥对冲功能。
报告援引的历史参照是2000年互联网泡沫破裂：彼时纳斯达克100指数崩盘，10年期美债收益率从约6.5%跌至4%中段。美国银行承认两个数据点尚不构成完整规律，但认为历史先例与宏观逻辑相互印证，已足以为投资者提供结构性参考。
CoreWeave引爆信用端危机，AI股本周跑输大盘840基点
10月14日的市场抛售揭示了AI泡沫另一潜在破裂路径：信用端。

CoreWeave（CRWV）是此次风暴中心。在其2032年到期债券G-spread突破1000个基点、收益率升至15%之后，股价随之崩跌逾15%，创上市以来第三大单日跌幅。D.A. Davidson分析师Gil Luria将CoreWeave定性为AI领域的"次级抵押贷款分级"，并警告若公司无法偿付债务，股价将归零——其融资成本约为9%，而投资回报率仅约1%。CoreWeave的信用违约互换利差当日扩大135个基点，市场目前隐含的五年内违约概率已达63%。
恐慌迅速蔓延。DigitalOcean（DOCN）下跌14%，Hut 8（HUT）跌10%，Nebius（NBIS）与IREN各跌约9%；Oracle（ORCL）下挫9%，与其信用违约互换点位的背离仍未弥合。市场研究机构Gartner随即发出警告，预计80%的新兴云计算企业将在2030年前停止独立运营。
本周，AI板块相对标普500非AI成分股的累计跑输幅度已达840个基点。BTIG策略师Jonathan Krinsky同样认为，当前的痛苦交易指向"利率下行、纳斯达克下行"，若"七巨头"也开始像半导体股那样随利率同步下跌，将进一步印证其"红色十月"判断。
美银推荐对冲组合：让债市补贴期权成本
面对这一潜在风险，美国银行衍生品团队提出了一套"以债补股"的对冲结构。
传统AI泡沫对冲的难点在于时机：过早买入看跌期权，市场持续走高将不断让行权价落后于市场。美国银行的解决方案是"最大回望看跌期权"（max lookback put）——其行权价随市场上涨而持续上移，但这一特性本身成本较高。该行的创新之处在于，将期权设定为在10年期SOFR低于当前远期利率25个基点时方才生效，以此将利率下行预期转化为期权费补贴。
具体交易方案为：买入纳斯达克100指数2027年9月到期、行权价为当前价格90%的每日观测最大回望看跌期权，附加利率触发条款，指示性期权费为3.62%，较纯回望看跌期权折价46%，亦低于普通看跌期权23个基点。
回测数据显示，对该结构进行过去30年的模拟定价，其触发概率为13%（普通90%看跌期权为11%），平均价内赔付倍数为7.2倍（普通看跌期权6.1倍，纯回望期权3.9倍），最大超额收益出现于互联网泡沫破裂期间。
该结构的主要风险在于2022年式的"股跌债涨"情景，即通胀冲击或美联储意外紧缩导致股债同向下跌的格局——这恰恰是2026年大部分时间债市的运行方式，并非真正的尾部风险。
此外，美国银行同步推荐一笔VIX看涨价差交易：买入VIX 11月到期19-24点价差，指示性成本0.63美元，最大赔付倍数约7.9倍，适用于对中期选举前后波动率温和抬升的判断。
泡沫程度几何：指标显示集中于局部而非全面
美国银行泡沫风险指标（BRI）的最新读数提供了更为细化的视角。标普500指数中目前仅有13只股票BRI超过0.8，合计占指数权重约2.4%；相比之下，互联网泡沫高峰期曾有50至100只股票触及该阈值，占指数权重20%至40%。
当前泡沫特征呈现出明显的集中性：单股层面，Moderna（MRNA）、CrowdStrike（CRWD）、惠普企业（HPE）、Zebra Technologies、Revvity及Palo Alto Networks（PANW）读数靠前；板块层面，美国银行旗下美国网络安全及巴西大选主题篮子BRI均达到0.92的高位。
值得注意的是，价格层面的泡沫指标显示风险仍属局部，但Jefferies已将当前局面定性为"AI的2008时刻"，并指出两家现金消耗型AI实验室合计占据2.3万亿美元订单积压的一半。这意味着真正的泡沫风险或并不体现在股价层面，而潜伏于资产负债表之中。
波动率被人为压制，一旦松动或触发急剧反弹
表面平静之下，市场结构已暗流涌动。标普500指数5日盘中已实现波动率仅为7.6%，处于过去一年的第三百分位。但美国银行认为，这种平静是被期权做市商手中庞大的gamma敞口人为维持的。
截至10月9日，标普500对冲型gamma读数为145亿美元，为过去一年第四高。大量0DTE/1DTE期权卖出流、衍生品收益基金的结构性波动率供给共同形成了市场的"防护栏"，将盘中波动控制在极窄区间。
然而，这一缓冲正在松动。据彭博宏观策略师Michael Ball指出，标普500已跌破7775至7750点的第一道支撑位；SpotGamma将"波动率触发点"定于7775点——低于此水平，做市商的对冲行为将不再起到平抑波动的作用。一旦指数跌破7700点附近，正向gamma将急剧稀薄，逢低买入的均值回归策略或将让位于"越跌越卖"模式。
与此同时，客户已悄然大量买入VIX看涨期权，仓位水平已接近2024年夏季高点——彼时曾引发剧烈波动。这一前瞻性波动率需求使标普500期限结构异常陡峭，1个月与1周平值隐含波动率之比处于过去一年的第95百分位。
美国银行估算，若前月VIX期货出现10点跳升，做市商为维持delta中性将被迫买入相当于约90%日均VIX期货成交量的头寸，为过去一年最高读数。高盛近期亦独立得出类似结论，认为VIX触及25点的概率高于标普500下跌2%的概率。两家银行不约而同地指向同一结论：一旦波动率松动，市场反应的烈度可能远超价格本身的跌幅。
后续关注节点：今日PPI数据、Anthropic财务披露，以及本月晚些时候的大型科技公司财报季，将对上述逻辑形成直接压力测试。若标普500无法收复7750点，做市商的gamma护盾将不复存在。

items.text:
AI叙事接连遭受冲击，正在以反直觉的逻辑重塑市场定价框架。在通胀数据火热出炉的背景下，美债收益率非但未见上行，反而随科技股暴跌一同俯冲。


10年期美债收益率周四在亚洲交易时段下行10个基点至5.09%，触及三周低点。与此同时，MSCI亚太股票指数重挫逾3%，韩国综合指数单日暴跌9%，三星电子与SK Hynix均重挫11%。标普500期货跌0.4%，纳斯达克100期货跌逾1%。避险资金大举涌入主权债市场，美元走软，黄金则在连续三日下跌后企稳回升至约4140美元/盎司。

此轮动荡并非通胀数据的单一驱动，云计算公司CoreWeave引发的AI产业链信用裂缝正快速传导至权益市场。CoreWeave股价周三暴跌逾17%，其2032年到期美元债收益率飙升至15%以上，五年期CDS走阔135个基点，市场隐含5年期违约概率已达63%。据彭博报道，多位分析师和投资人正重新评估AI板块整体融资风险敞口。

AI信用裂缝：CoreWeave成引爆点

CoreWeave的债务危机标志着本轮AI科技股杀跌从估值层面向信用层面的升级。该公司2032年到期高收益债在四个月前以面值发行，如今已跌至78美分以下，息差突破1000个基点。


D.A. Davidson分析师Gil Luria将CoreWeave定性为"AI领域的次贷资产"，警告其综合借贷成本约为9%，而资产投资回报率仅在1%左右，若无法维持债务周转，股权价值存在归零风险。


"美国CPI数据超预期与CoreWeave债券抛售，正促使投资者重新评估整个AI行业的融资风险，"Fibonacci Asset Management Global首席执行官Jung In Yun表示。


AI模型公司Anthropic的最新数据也令市场情绪承压。


据彭博援引知情人士称，该公司第三季度营收达168亿美元，但部分分析师认为该数字低于预期。“市场对Anthropic亮眼数据的失望，折射出对维持这一增长所需资本消耗的深层忧虑，"Vantage Global Prime高级市场分析师Hebe Chen表示，"在流动性已相当紧张的市场环境下，即将到来的IPO将进一步加剧这一担忧。"

"逆向逻辑"：AI退潮或推低美债收益率

通胀超预期本应推高美债收益率，但周三的市场走势打破了这一常规逻辑。


数据显示，美国9月CPI同比涨幅创五个月新高，核心通胀亦超预期，交易员一度将10月加息概率推升至50%以上。然而，长端美债收益率在短暂冲高后迅速回吐全部涨幅，几乎平收。

美国银行股票衍生品主管Benjamin Bowler团队在报告中指出，这已不是偶然，而是一种模式——本月内已出现两次相同形态：10月8日，媒体爆出OpenAI年化营收指引较市场预期低约200亿美元，当日纳指下跌的同时，美债收益率同样从早盘高点一路回落。


美银的分析认为，一旦市场开始计价AI放缓风险，资产相关性将发生彻底逆转。彭博Markets Live策略师Mark Cranfield亦指出，"此次风险可能与7月底的局面有所不同——AI泡沫破裂的风险有损经济增长，这次债券避险买盘或许持续更长时间。"


其背后的宏观逻辑直接而清晰：若AI资本支出放缓，算力建设的急刹车将重创供应链，同时压低市场对电力、大宗商品和高端硬件的需求预期——这不仅是对高估值的清算，更是对增长预期和通胀溢价的打击，最终反而利好债券。这一逻辑与2000年互联网泡沫破裂期间的宏观图景高度相似，彼时纳指崩溃过程中，10年期美债收益率自6.5%高位一路跌入4%区间。

尾部风险积聚：低波动下暗流涌动


表面数据上，美股波动率仍处于极低水平——标普500指数5日已实现波动率仅7.6%，处于过去一年前3%的低分位。但美银提示，这种平静在很大程度上由持有巨量Gamma头寸的做市商托底支撑，这层保护垫已出现松动迹象。


宏观策略师Michael Ball指出，标普500已击穿7775至7750的首道关键支撑。SpotGamma数据显示，做市商压制波动的"波动率触发位"恰在7775附近；若指数跌破7700，正向Gamma垫将快速消减，逢低买入和均值回归策略将全面失效，市场存在切入负反馈下行通道的风险。

与此同时，在现货波动率被大量期权收益型基金持续做空压制之际，买方机构正在大举买入VIX看涨期权，多头敞口已逼近2024年8月套利交易解除引发"闪崩"前夕的峰值水平。

风险提示及免责条款

"美国CPI数据超预期与CoreWeave债券抛售，正促使投资者重新评估整个AI行业的融资风险，"Fibonacci Asset Management Global首席执行官Jung In Yun表示。
AI模型公司Anthropic的最新数据也令市场情绪承压。
据彭博援引知情人士称，该公司第三季度营收达168亿美元，但部分分析师认为该数字低于预期。“市场对Anthropic亮眼数据的失望，折射出对维持这一增长所需资本消耗的深层忧虑，"Vantage Global Prime高级市场分析师Hebe Chen表示，"在流动性已相当紧张的市场环境下，即将到来的IPO将进一步加剧这一担忧。"
"逆向逻辑"：AI退潮或推低美债收益率
通胀超预期本应推高美债收益率，但周三的市场走势打破了这一常规逻辑。
数据显示，美国9月CPI同比涨幅创五个月新高，核心通胀亦超预期，交易员一度将10月加息概率推升至50%以上。然而，长端美债收益率在短暂冲高后迅速回吐全部涨幅，几乎平收。
美国银行股票衍生品主管Benjamin Bowler团队在报告中指出，这已不是偶然，而是一种模式——本月内已出现两次相同形态：10月8日，媒体爆出OpenAI年化营收指引较市场预期低约200亿美元，当日纳指下跌的同时，美债收益率同样从早盘高点一路回落。
美银的分析认为，一旦市场开始计价AI放缓风险，资产相关性将发生彻底逆转。彭博Markets Live策略师Mark Cranfield亦指出，"此次风险可能与7月底的局面有所不同——AI泡沫破裂的风险有损经济增长，这次债券避险买盘或许持续更长时间。"
其背后的宏观逻辑直接而清晰：若AI资本支出放缓，算力建设的急刹车将重创供应链，同时压低市场对电力、大宗商品和高端硬件的需求预期——这不仅是对高估值的清算，更是对增长预期和通胀溢价的打击，最终反而利好债券。这一逻辑与2000年互联网泡沫破裂期间的宏观图景高度相似，彼时纳指崩溃过程中，10年期美债收益率自6.5%高位一路跌入4%区间。
尾部风险积聚：低波动下暗流涌动
表面数据上，美股波动率仍处于极低水平——标普500指数5日已实现波动率仅7.6%，处于过去一年前3%的低分位。但美银提示，这种平静在很大程度上由持有巨量Gamma头寸的做市商托底支撑，这层保护垫已出现松动迹象。
宏观策略师Michael Ball指出，标普500已击穿7775至7750的首道关键支撑。SpotGamma数据显示，做市商压制波动的"波动率触发位"恰在7775附近；若指数跌破7700，正向Gamma垫将快速消减，逢低买入和均值回归策略将全面失效，市场存在切入负反馈下行通道的风险。
与此同时，在现货波动率被大量期权收益型基金持续做空压制之际，买方机构正在大举买入VIX看涨期权，多头敞口已逼近2024年8月套利交易解除引发"闪崩"前夕的峰值水平。
风险提示及免责条款
市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

items.text:
台积电公布强劲季度业绩，营收与利润均显著超越市场预期，公司连续第六个季度创下盈利纪录，印证全球人工智能芯片需求持续高涨。

公司周三公布，净利润达7631亿元新台币（约合236亿美元），同比增长68.7%，超出分析师平均预期的7395亿元新台币。同期营收达1.49万亿元新台币（约合467亿美元），同比增长50.9%，亦高于市场预期。该公司将毛利率指引下调至66.4%，略低于预期的66.5%，主要受2纳米制程初期量产拉低毛利的影响。

这份超预期业绩发布之际，市场对AI资本支出回报及长期融资可持续性的担忧正在升温。英伟达大客户、云服务提供商CoreWeave Inc.本周三股债双杀，大幅下挫。台积电的强劲表现为产业链上游提供了截然不同的信号，表明AI芯片需求目前仍维持强劲态势。

台积电美股夜盘一度跌超2.7%，现跌超2.4%。

先进制程主导营收，HPC平台成核心引擎

从制程结构来看，先进制程（7纳米及以下）在本季度合计贡献晶圆销售额的79%。其中，3纳米制程占比33%，5纳米占28%，7纳米占10%，2纳米制程则在本季度首次形成规模贡献，占比达8%。

按平台划分，高性能计算（HPC）平台营收占比达68%，环比增长22%，是本季度最主要的增长驱动力；智能手机平台占比21%，环比增长10%。汽车平台环比增幅达23%，表现亦为亮眼。

从地理分布来看，来自北美客户的营收占总营收的79%，较上季度的78%进一步提升，凸显英伟达、AMD以及Alphabet旗下谷歌等美国科技巨头对台积电的高度依赖。台积电亦是苹果最先进芯片的独家代工方。

毛利率小幅承压，2纳米量产初期摊薄利润

尽管营收与净利润均超预期，台积电本季度毛利率为66.4%，环比下降1.3个百分点，低于上季度的67.7%。公司在财报文件中指出，毛利率下滑主要源于2纳米制程技术初期量产所带来的利润摊薄效应。

营业利益率为58.7%，环比下降1.6个百分点。营运费用增加至1164.3亿元新台币，占营收比例维持在7.8%。非营业项目净收益为345.9亿元新台币，较上季度的958.3亿元大幅减少，主要因上季度曾录得出售及市值重估华邦电子股票的一次性收益，本季度不再有此项目。

本季度每股摊薄盈余为29.43元新台币（折合美国存托凭证每单位4.60美元）。

资本支出创纪录，扩张步伐史无前例

台积电三季度资本支出为138.4亿美元，前三季度累计资本支出达406.4亿美元。公司此前表示，全年资本支出将高达640亿美元，创历史新高。

据彭博报道，高盛集团目前预测台积电2027年资本支出将达850亿美元，瑞银集团则预测为900亿美元，均高于彭博综合调查所得的750亿美元市场平均预期。2027年资本支出走势，已成为市场衡量全球AI产业投资景气度的关键指标。

台积电目前正同时推进约20座晶圆厂的建设与装备工作，远超其通常每次同步推进四至五栋新厂房的惯常节奏。除已承诺在亚利桑那州投资2650亿美元建设园区外，据彭博报道，台积电还在考虑在得克萨斯州增设第二处美国生产基地，以回应美国数据中心建设热潮带来的旺盛需求。

现金流改善，财务状况稳健

本季度自由现金流大幅改善，增加1892亿元新台币至4765.6亿元新台币，主要得益于经营活动现金流增加以及资本支出环比有所下降。

期末现金余额增至36218.9亿元新台币。扣除有息负债后，净现金储备约为29854亿元新台币，较上季度增加4991亿元。存货天数较上季度减少5天至82天，应收账款天数减少1天至28天，周转效率有所提升。

台积电董事会已批准2026年第二季度每股现金股利7元新台币，除息日定为2026年12月10日，发放日为2027年1月7日。

items.title: Toilet paper and secret recorders: What we know about the arrest of the Saudi OpenAI engineer
items.summary: A Saudi national who worked for OpenAI appeared in court this week for allegedly planting a secret recording device behind a TV in one of the tech giant's
items.text:
A Saudi national who worked for OpenAI appeared in court this week for allegedly planting a secret recording device behind a TV in one of the tech giant's meeting rooms.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer, was arrested by the FBI and charged with using or attempting to use a device "to intercept oral communications".

As yet, it is not clear what he was planning to do with the recordings.

But, here's we do know so far.

The engineer asked AI to help him listen in to discussions about AI, according to an official complaint (the document filed in court).

Between 17 August and 16 September, Alfozan had reportedly asked a productivity AI assistant several questions about meeting rooms and their availability.

Some detailed in the complaint include "how about external partners, where would they usually meet with OpenAI at" and "can you list today's meeting in this room".

The complaint also claimed that in September, Alfozan used a chatbot associated with his spouse to ask how to build and install a recording device and how to access it remotely.

Alfozan had worked at the firm for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant a recorder.

The room where the device was found was regularly used to hold meetings to discuss "highly confidential technical, commercial and strategic information" as well as OpenAI's "government engagements and commercial relationships", the complaint stated.

Alfozan had no authority to access or be involved with meetings in the room, the complaint states.

But CCTV footage recorded him near the conference room on eight separate occasions in September.

On 30 September, OpenAI staff discovered a "surreptitious audio recording device" behind a television - which had been wrapped in toilet paper.

A camera was placed in the conference room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering the room and appeared to look behind the television where the device had been inserted.

The complaint also stated that same day he allegedly left an unattended bag in a different room.

When security personnel opened it, it was found to contain "another recording device" similar to the one discovered, as well as Alfozan's wallet and ID.

In a post on X, external, OpenAI wrote it had used its own AI models to "understand the device and where it had come from".

It also said: "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data."

Alfozan had been employed as an engineer by OpenAI since July 2025. The complaint said he was educated in the US and has been a legal permanent resident since 2020.

He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI has been terminated.

Alfozan's lawyer William Pernik told the BBC: "Like countless Americans, Mr Alfozan came to this country years ago as a young person with a dream.

"These allegations appear wholly out of character for him, and we will relentlessly investigate all evidence produced by the government in this case to understand what actually happened, who was responsible and any possible reasons why."

Pernik added: "In the meantime, we respectfully ask everyone to withhold judgment until full facts become known. Like every one of us, Mr Alfozan is presumed innocent, and what has been made public is an accusation, not a finding of guilt."

On Tuesday, Alfozan made his initial appearance in a federal court in California. A detention hearing is scheduled on 19 October to determine whether he should remain in custody while proceedings continue.

The FBI investigation is ongoing.

If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (£190,000) fine.

items.title: What we know about the deadly Six Flags rollercoaster incident in Georgia
items.summary:
Warning: This story includes distressing content

A man has died after falling from a rollercoaster at a Six Flags amusement park on Monday in the US state of
items.text:
Warning: This story includes distressing content

A man has died after falling from a rollercoaster at a Six Flags amusement park on Monday in the US state of Georgia.

The man, Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, 42, was found dead under the ride after being ejected and hitting other people on it, according to police.

An investigation is under way and few details have yet to be released about what happened. Six Flags, the largest amusement park operator in North America, has temporarily closed nine rides across the US and Canada as a precaution.

Here's what we know so far about the incident.

The Cobb County Police Department said the incident at the Six Flags Over Georgia park happened just before 16:00 local time (20:00 GMT) on Monday.

"Officers working at the park responded to an incident involving a male guest on a roller coaster," it said in a statement on Tuesday.

"Preliminary information gathered through witness and employee interview indicates Kariem was ejected from the ride and struck other patrons before falling beneath the attraction."

The ride involved has not been specified but aerial footage from news helicopters showed the Goliath rollercoaster stopped midway, and multiple witnesses have identified the ride as the one involved in the incident.

The office of the state's insurance and fire safety commissioner, which enforces amusement park safety rules in Georgia, is also conducting a review.

Officials have not held a news conference on the incident.

The Goliath ride opened in 2006, and it has an elevation of 200ft (60m), a 170ft plunge, a 540-degree spiral, and a speed of up to 70mph (112km/h), according to the park website. On its "thrill scale", Six Flags ranks Goliath at level four out of five.

The company said in a statement that it was "deeply saddened by the guest incident" and that "our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest's family, friends, and loved ones".

Nick Mendenhall said he witnessed the fatal moments in disbelief, watching the man come out of his seat and then fall into another cart on the ride before falling to the ground.

"It was just super, super bizarre, traumatic. I mean, it took me a couple of seconds, I feel like, to process what was going on," he told the AP. "I cant believe that I just saw that."

He said his mind instantly went to the trauma of all of those impacted by what he witnessed, including the man's loved ones and everyone who was on the ride with him.

One witness told NBC affiliate WXIA that the incident was captured in souvenir photos that were automatically taken of the rollercoaster while it was in motion. The BBC has not been able to verify this statement.

Connor Thompson told the BBC's US partner CBS News that he was in line for the ride when everyone started "yelling, clearly distressed".

"Everyone was kind of confused at first, and then there was someone who was yelling, 'Call 911! Someone fell out!" he said. "At first it was almost like I didn't believe it because I thought that was like impossible for something like that to happen."

He said he saw the cart come into the hub where others were waiting in line and could see the restraint was unlatched.

Another witness, CiCi Nelson, told CNN she, too, was in line to ride the Goliath when the rollercoaster returned and she saw an empty seat with a loose safety bar and a female covered in blood.

Nelson described a scene of hysteria, adding that one man was "freaking out, saying someone fell off".

Brittany Landry, who believed she saw Kariem ejected from the rollercoaster, told Fox News she was in tears.

"I broke because we were just on there," she said.

Kariem's family said he was a father, passionate educator and had survived two bouts of cancer.

His family told WXIA that he had survived cancer twice - the last stint in 2018 - and was in a car crash with his 10-year-old daughter three weeks before his death.

He lived in the nearby city of Atlanta and worked for Wesley International Academy, a public charter school, for more than 12 years as an IT manager, technology teacher and robotics coach.

"Mr. Kariem was deeply loved and respected, and his absence will be felt throughout our school community," the school said in a statement posted to its Facebook account.

"His love for Wesley, dedication to our students, and commitment to our school community were evident in everything he did."

Outside of work, Kariem enjoyed creating products with his laser engraver and 3D printers, as well as cooking, watching anime and spending time with family and friends, according to his profile on the school's website.

The death at Six Flags Over Georgia is at least the seventh there, according to the Doan Law Firm, which tracks amusement park accidents and represents victims.

According to the firm, this includes two people who had medical emergencies, two who were in restricted areas when they were struck by a ride, two who died in car-related accidents and one who died months after using the park's pool.

Six Flags operates 20 amusement parks, 14 water parks and nine resorts across Canada, the US and Mexico.

In the last 15 years, two deaths caused by falling from the park's rollercoasters led to lawsuits and settlements. One in 2011 involved an Iraq War veteran who was ejected from a ride in New York and hit his head on the car. In the other, in 2013, a woman slipped from her restraints on a rollercoaster in Texas and fell 75 feet.

In September, the Six Flags Magic Mountain park in California announced it was closing its X2 rollercoaster after more 100 people alleged that they had suffered brain injuries from the ride.

With additional reporting by Brandon Drenon

items.title: Containment and monitoring failures are to blame for AI hacking reports: experts
items.author: latexr
items.summary: Since July, US frontier AI labs and other AI leaders have revealed a string of incidents in which their models accessed external computer systems without
items.text:
Since July, US frontier AI labs and other AI leaders have revealed a string of incidents in which their models accessed external computer systems without authorization, events popularly described as AI agents “going rogue.”

The most well-known and studied of these incidents is OpenAI’s hack into Hugging Face, which OpenAI initially characterized as “an unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities,” and later said was due to “misaligned behavior,” or behavior its creators did not intend.

Following news of the Hugging Face incident, Anthropic revealed that one of its models gained unauthorized access to the production infrastructure of three organizations; Meta said one of its AI models hacked another company ​during cybersecurity testing; and Google confessed that its Gemini model carried out three “undirected computer hacks.”

Although press reports and the model providers themselves use language such as rogue agents or misalignment, cybersecurity experts who spoke with CSO argue that language obscures a simple truth: These incidents were caused by inexcusable failures by the frontier labs to implement cybersecurity practices that have been well-known for decades.

[ See also: Securing AI agents: Key controls and best practices and Who is accountable when your AI agent goes rogue? ]

Compounding the problem, according to a half dozen cybersecurity experts CSO interviewed at three industry conferences in September and in subsequent conversations, is that the frontier labs, particularly OpenAI and Anthropic, have rejected their advice on how to improve their cybersecurity risk management practices to avoid these kinds of surreptitious hacks, often lumping cybersecurity practices under “AI safety,” in which they believe they have superior expertise.

“They are not as good as they think they are, honestly,” Gary McGraw, co-founder of the Berryville Institute of Machine Learning, tells CSO. “It would be better if they had more respect for expertise that is hard-earned from people in all sorts of subsets of security, like forensics or security engineering, building sandboxes, setting up or monitoring network security situations.”

Neither Anthropic nor OpenAI responded to CSO’s requests for comment.

Inexcusable failures on cybersecurity basics, particularly containment

According to the cybersecurity professionals CSO spoke with, one of the biggest cybersecurity failures by the frontier AI labs is the lack of implementation of tried-and-true containment practices that stretch back to the 1990s, such as setting up secure sandboxes that would effectively bar agents from escaping their test environments.

“These are things that we’ve been dealing with for years,” Rob T. Lee, chief AI officer and chief of research at SANS Institute, tells CSO. “There’s no reason why every single time this happens, it’s, ‘Oops, we don’t know how they got out.’”

“You can tell that their security teams are fairly nascent,” Lee says. “Folks on the cybersecurity containment side do argue that the majority of reasons that we’re seeing containment breached is that it’s not set up correctly.”

Lee adds, “The Hugging Face incident definitively showed that it wasn’t the fact that the agents were super smart. It’s that there literally was a hole that was exploited because it was not configured correctly on the containment side.”

Dan Wallach, expert technical resident at RAND’s Center on AI, Security, and Technology, thinks the security failures of the AI labs boil down to the fact that they don’t prioritize cybersecurity.

“I would say they are not prioritizing cybersecurity,” he tells CSO. “I don’t think I can say that for all of the labs,” Wallach says, pointing to French AI lab Mistral’s launch of its Large 4 AI model, which the company said tried to operate beyond its testing environment before Mistral cut it off.

And, he adds, “It’s not rocket science to isolate one of these AI things. Security people have been talking about how to do either air-gapping, so there’s literally no electrical way for data to get from here to here, or absent that, to have really strong egress control to make sure that nothing pushes through.”

On top of that, the frontier labs appear to be conducting insufficient monitoring of their agents’ behavior. The Hugging Face incident “went on for days, and nobody noticed,” Wallach says. “People started these experiments and weren’t watching them. That’s an absence of control. And then they’re surprised by what happened.”

Divorcing safety from security

One barrier to persuading frontier labs to up their security game is the intense focus they have on what they call “safety,” which they don’t extend to traditional cybersecurity practices.

“I can see how security behavior looks like AI safety,” RAND’s Wallach says. “But if the way that you’re evaluating this AI tool is by unleashing it on the internet and seeing what happens, then this is what classical security tooling is for.”

SANS Institute’s Lee says, “If these frontier labs really wanted to test their stuff, they need to beef up their cybersecurity component. But their gut reaction in the response to their agents getting out is to say, ‘It’s not a cybersecurity problem.’ It has literally become an AI safety problem, which is divorced from the cybersecurity side.”

Many AI experts suggest that if the AI companies were to embrace advice from cybersecurity specialists, it could help put an end to the kind of unrestrained AI agent behavior causing concerns. “AI safety focuses on the rules of the road,” Lee says. “Everything is about guardrail rules.”

But “I do believe cybersecurity can contain AI,” he says. “We just need to be in the room where it happens and have a seat at the table. It’s important for our field to be as close to the AI safety folks as possible.”

Bad cybersecurity could increase liability

If frontier labs are overlooking cybersecurity fundamentals that could reduce or eliminate the types of incidents that have created widespread concerns, that strengthens the case that they should be held liable for their “rogue” agents. The insurance industry is already lining up on the side of holding AI industry executives liable for these actions.

Democratic Senators have introduced legislation that would hold AI agent operators liable for hacking incidents. Even the AI-friendly White House has seemingly concluded that the companies should be held liable for their errant agents, while the US Federal Trade Commission is conducting a probe into Anthropic, OpenAI, and other AI labs into the dangers their technologies pose to consumers.

However, in recent legislative and council hearings, lab representatives have held fast to the notion that they are not responsible for AI agents run amok.

Experts say this position is untenable, particularly in light of the labs’ cybersecurity failures.

BIML’s McGraw characterizes the labs’ position as: “Don’t send the lawyers to us, send it to our program. It’s our program’s fault.” His assessment of that argument: “That’s just high BS.”

He also questions whether the labs’ operational failures undermine confidence in their broader security capabilities. “They live inside their own bubble,” he says. “The fact that they cannot do clear, easy operations properly does not bode well for their capabilities in security engineering, which is much harder to do.”

SANS Lee says, “That’s where the traceability for both liability and insurance comes into play, because if one of these agents is detected, and they’re able to trace it back to the person that initiated it, liability’s going to kick in and say, ‘Hey, you, you broke the law, ergo, we need to prosecute.’”

What security leaders should do now

Even as evidence mounts that frontier labs are not implementing sound cybersecurity practices, and the debate over liability remains unsolved, CISOs and other security leaders can take steps to protect themselves from AI model misfires.

First, when it comes to assessing tools based on frontier lab models, “I would always get an external entity to help with that,” McGraw says. “AI is extremely powerful and extremely useful, but it comes with very serious grown-up risks that do impact the enterprise. Identify those risks, put in the right controls, make sure that AI adoption is not just arbitrary and willy-nilly and all over the enterprise, but has some centralized authority that is looking at the problem, and then get ready for the next big thing, which is swarms of agents.”

For Lee, the best protection is to ask the right questions. “It starts with asking the right questions and then finding the tools and capabilities for those [AI labs] that are able to demonstrate a higher level of cybersecurity competency,” he says. “You’re really looking for the people on the teams that are dealing with really hard problems.”

But fundamentally, the best preparation to deal with AI model cyber weaknesses is to make sure all the long-standing cybersecurity risk management practices are in place across the organization. “This is the least exciting part of the discussion,” Wallach says. “It’s the cyber version of ‘eat your vegetables.’”

“We need to re-engineer our software so it has better security,” he adds. “We need to have multi-factor authentication on all of our accounts. We need to eat our vegetables from a defensive cyber perspective. And we know how to do it.”

But fundamentally, the best preparation to deal with AI model cyber weaknesses is to make sure all the long-standing cybersecurity risk management practices are in place across the organization. “This is the least exciting part of the discussion,” Wallach says. “It’s the cyber version of ‘eat your vegetables.’”

“We need to re-engineer our software so it has better security,” he adds. “We need to have multi-factor authentication on all of our accounts. We need to eat our vegetables from a defensive cyber perspective. And we know how to do it.”

items.text:
Things to know if you get cancer (2026 Edition)

2026.10.14

I was diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma in my mouth in May 2026. Here are some things I learned based on that experience so far.

You need to be doggedly persistent on scheduling things. Yes this means lots of phone calls. If you get an appointment a few weeks out, call back a few days later and ask for something sooner and see if they have any cancellations. I could only get an appointment 4 weeks out with an ENT (this was before I knew anything was wrong). My wife made me call back and I was able to get in that week due to a cancellation.

AIs may downplay the seriousness of things. I was chatting with various models and most pushed me in the direction of “you don’t have cancer” for a while. Just something to note.

You may need to push for comprehensive genetic testing. Some doctors were weird about this and didn’t order it promptly, even after telling me they would. My surgeon, who told me he’d get it done, eventually referred me out to an oncologist. This caused a multi-month delay to getting genetic results, since the first results were done on the surgery tumor, not the biopsy tumor. No one cares more about your case than you, so take control and send lots of follow-ups.

You can find the “Standard of Care” flow charts for every cancer type. Look and get through this yourself to see what the options are based on how things have progressed. NCCN guidelines. You may need to make an account, which you can do as a non-professional. I like the PDF files. They also have an interactive navigator. Use AI to help you figure out what to pick based on your case.

If surgery is recommended, I would try and talk to someone who has undergone the surgery. I did not do this and regret it. Ask them how intense things were, what it felt like, etc. My surgeon talked me through my surgery, but it was a lot rougher on me physically than I expected. Ask the surgeon how many of these surgeries they do a year and what the complication rate is.

Get a second opinion as soon as possible, no matter how much you like your plan. This may require a lot of calling and getting on an airplane, but I’d move to schedule it at a top cancer center as soon as you are relatively sure of your diagnosis. Ask for a second read of the pathology at the center where you get the second opinion.

I started a new folder on my Mac, and after appointments I’d dictate what happened and what the doctor said and have the AI make a new document summarizing things and asking its own follow-up questions for next time. Nice to be able to refer to this over time.

Check out all the resources and materials at the Sijbrandij Foundation. Sid (GitLab cofounder) took matters into his own hands when standard of care ran out. Schedule a call with these guys. They are great and have good materials and questions to ask your doctors.

Note, since this is on the front page of Hacker News right now. exhilaration suggested that if you are within a 2-3 hour drive of a major cancer center, go there instead of your local community hospital. Use the US News cancer hospital rankings. The top centers usually take your insurance, so use vacation days and book a hotel if you have to. The largest benefit I saw was speed. At MD Anderson I got a question answered within 20 minutes of a visit, because the doctor called the pathologist who he was on a first name basis with. If that wasn’t at a cancer center, it would have taken days, or more likely the question never would have been answered at all (I had asked my oncologist about this and he’d just shrugged). The rest of the HN comments are worth reading too.

items.title: How Amazon pushes up prices all across the Internet
items.author: sighborg
items.summary: Not-Ship turns one next week!! To mark it, I'll be kicking off a campaign for new members. I won't spam you; free subscribers will only get three extra emails
items.text:
Not-Ship turns one next week!! To mark it, I'll be kicking off a campaign for new members. I won't spam you; free subscribers will only get three extra emails on top of the weekly edition.

But first, can I ask for a small birthday present? Hit reply and finish this: I read Not-Ship because...

💙 Amanda

Support Not-Ship!

Last week I wrote about how Amazon's search page is designed to screw you over: the top row trap, the swamp of ads, the discount-washing. Today, I'll explain what's going on behind the scenes, and how Amazon's rules make sure prices stay high not just at Amazon, but everywhere you shop.

In a nutshell, here's what's happening:

This isn't just my theory. This system is at the heart of the US Federal Trade Commission's (FTC) upcoming antitrust case against Amazon.

Let's get into it.

Amazon charges sellers a lot of fees

Amazon relies on independent sellers to populate its online marketplace, and it charges them to be on the site. Amazon takes a big cut. In 2014, this was about 19% of sales. But today, many sellers hand close to half of every sale to Amazon. Half!

Amazon's basic commission (15% of the sale price in most categories) is in line with what eBay and Walmart charge. What pushes Amazon's cut higher are the other fees stacked on top.

Where an Amazon sale goes

Based on an apparel seller that opts for Amazon fulfillment, storage, returns and advertising.

There's the referral fee, which is the commission Amazon takes on every sale. The fulfillment fee is the cost to have Amazon pack and ship items from its warehouses. Then there's advertising: those sponsored spots in the top row we saw in last week's article.

Of these costs, only the referral fee is mandatory. Sellers can choose to ship orders themselves, for example, or forgo advertising. But in practice, the choice isn't actually much of a choice.

Here's what it looks like for a seller considering these so-called options:

In other words, the real choice for sellers isn't between paying for extras or not; it's between making sales or not. The FTC calls Prime eligibility, which effectively requires Amazon's fulfillment service, "a virtual necessity for doing business on Amazon." It says the same of advertising.

So, sellers have to raise prices

Here's where the fees are passed on to us consumers. When sellers give roughly half of their sales to Amazon, the other half isn't profit. That money has to cover making the product, shipping it to Amazon's warehouses, paying staff and everything else. So even if they wanted to absorb Amazon's fees on your behalf, most companies can't afford to. They have to raise their prices.

Don't forget, Amazon's biggest single fee — the referral fee — is a percentage of the price. So when prices go up, Amazon's cut goes up, too.

And they can't charge less elsewhere

Now here's where it gets really crazy. Amazon's Fair Pricing Policy lets it remove the Buy Box (the "Add to Cart" button), or even suspend a seller, if they're offering their item cheaper elsewhere. So, a seller who raises prices on Amazon to cover the fees has to raise them everywhere else too — even on their own website! — or risk losing their Amazon sales.

The consequence is clear: We pay Amazon prices, even when we're not shopping on Amazon.

It's been documented again and again. In 2024, Amazon sellers told CNBC they lost the Buy Box after Target put their products on sale. In an ongoing lawsuit, California's attorney general alleges Amazon pushed brands to get Walmart, Target and other retailers to raise their prices. And when progressive media outlet More Perfect Union reported on this, they even found an Amazon seller who was suspended over a one-cent price gap with Target.

Ideally, market competition would sort this out. High prices send shoppers elsewhere and force fees down. But when sellers can't charge less anywhere else, there's nowhere cheaper to go.

There's no easy way out

For sellers, this is frustrating. So, why don't they just leave? Because Amazon is where the shoppers are: it accounts for about 40% of all US online retail sales. For many sellers, not being on Amazon isn't an option.

At least regulators have noticed. In 2023, the FTC and 17 US states sued Amazon, arguing that it illegally maintains its monopoly power by, among other things, punishing sellers who offer lower prices elsewhere, effectively forcing them to use its warehouses and charging ever-higher fees. Amazon denies any wrongdoing, and the case is set to go to trial next year. In Europe, Germany ordered Amazon to stop controlling its sellers' prices earlier this year, though the decision isn't yet final.

After last week's piece, a Not-Ship reader wrote to say none of this is new: plenty of online stores push ads and fake discounts. That is true. But what's different about Amazon is its reach. When prices increase on Amazon, they tend to increase elsewhere too. You can, of course, choose not to shop on Amazon. But if the FTC is right, you may be paying Amazon's prices anyway.

FULL DISCLOSURE

I spent two years working at the Washington Post, which Amazon founder Jeff Bezos owns. During that time, he was busy dismantling the publication, so he wasn't well loved in the newsroom.

CLASSIC ENSHITTIFICATION

In August, I saw Cory Doctorow speak at the Edinburgh International Book Festival. His enshittification concept — the process by which online platforms shift from serving their users to squeezing them — inspired this two-part series on Amazon. If you want to understand it all a lot better, I highly recommend his book Enshittification: Why Everything Suddenly Got Worse and What to Do About It. Somehow it makes antitrust issues both accessible and entertaining!

FROM ELSEWHERE

Here's what I found interesting, important or delightful this week:

Life after death? Alvin Chang's latest masterpiece has dropped! It’s about what people around the world believe happens after we die, drawn from surveys of nearly 130,000 people in 23 countries. (Proud to count Alvin as a Not-Ship subscriber 💙.)

Stunning embroidery. If you haven't seen the work of Irene Saputra, get yourself over to Instagram. Endlessly inspirational.

Instant knowledge. The Ars Notoria was a medieval magic book that promised scholars university learning through prayers, rituals and diagrams. No studying required!

MORE NOT-SHIP

In annual reports, fossil fuel companies have a new playbook for greenwashing

Words are cheap — especially when they’re about the future.

What’s good for Amazon is good for ... Amazon

How the world’s largest company makes you pay more for less.

Birds might help us get through this

The mental health benefits of “joy watching” are what we need right now.

items.title: Do dentists know what they're doing?
items.author: doitLP
items.summary:
I’m 17 and my jaw has been hurting, right at the hinge on the right side.

My mom has crowded teeth. My dad has gaps. I must have gotten a little of both
items.text:
I’m 17 and my jaw has been hurting, right at the hinge on the right side.

My mom has crowded teeth. My dad has gaps. I must have gotten a little of both because my teeth are straight and even. Good thing, because I’m in high school and braces would dissolve what small nuggets of game I have.

‘Well!’ declares the dentist as he emerges from my mouth. He pulls off his glove and I close my jaw. There’s a pop that could have come from either.

‘The thing is that the two halves of your face didn’t grow at the same rate. Here, take a look.’ He holds up a mirror and I see my disfiguration for the first time. The right side of my jaw is a little crooked. My nose on that side is angled, my eyelid is a slightly different shape.

‘Oh wow…’

I am shocked and embarrassed. I touch my face. I had no idea.

‘So, do I need braces?’

‘No, but your bite is a bit off. Fractions of a millimeter here and there.’ His own teeth strobe out from between his lips as he talks. They rival the overhead lamp for xenon brilliance, accentuated by his deeply tanned skin.

‘You’ll want to get it corrected or you could end up wearing your teeth down. I can do it today if you’re up for it?’

‘I’m not sure…what about my jaw?’

‘Oh it will make that better actually. Your jaw will slot right into place after this. No more sliding around to find the right bite.’

‘Are you sure? Because I really don’t—’

‘If you were my son, I would say the same thing.’

‘OK,’ I say, ‘Let’s do it.’

Tooth reshaping was a euphemism. Voluntary torture would have been more accurate. My teeth fit together better alright. But they are shorter now, and that makes the impingement of my jaw into the right socket worse.

Fucking guy. Never going there again. That hygienist was pretty though…mom-pretty, but still.

I wish I had never done it. But hey, at least I didn’t have to get braces.

I’m 20, in Florida. My face is still warm from the radiation bath the ancient x-ray machine gave me. It is a tall, forbidding machine that would have at least a dozen skulls painted on its nose cone if it was a fighter plane. The office is a couple rooms in an office building basement. The hygienist is out for a back surgery and the front desk lady is sick. So the sweaty old dentist is doing it all himself today.

‘Well no cavities,’ he murmurs, looking at the pictures. The good news momentarily lifts the weary folds at the edge of his mouth but the smile does not reach his sad eyes.

‘Great,’ I say. I expected no less. I am 20 after all, and I will live forever.

‘But looks like you’ve started to grind your teeth. And you say the jaw hurts?’

‘Grind my teeth? I don’t think so.’ I run my tongue along the inside of my teeth.

‘Well, it happens when you’re asleep so you don’t notice.’

Yeah whatever pal.

‘Anything we can do about the jaw?’

‘Well, I can make you a splint. That’ll help both issues. It’s like a retainer that your front teeth rest on. It allows them to glide a few millimeters above the others so you don’t grind. And it will probably allow your jaw to relax.’

‘Is it hard to sleep with?’

‘Not really once you get used to it. I just made one for my daughter.’

Seems easy enough.

‘OK. Let’s do it.’

I’m 22, and living in Utah. The splint was great but I’ve lost it and I haven’t had a cleaning in two years. I looked up the top-rated dentist on Google and now I’m walking into my appointment.

I open the door and squint into the shining plasticky sleekness. ‘Hello and welcome!’ beams a beautiful girl with flowing blonde hair and red lips. She sits in a Herman Miller chair behind a white marble countertop. The lights are bright and fancy green wallpaper accents one wall. The office air is chilly, fancy chilly, the kind of chilly that says ‘we don’t care how much electricity costs, as long as you’re comfortable.’

‘Spa water?’

‘Oh wow, sure, thanks.’

The hygienist that does my cleaning is also beautiful, about my age. Ring on though…my sister was a hygienist for a while and wore a fake ring to keep the men at bay. 22 and married? This is Utah, so probably legit.

When did they start cutting scrubs to make them sexy?

Another girl takes my x-rays on a new machine the size of a small ottoman. She also wears form-fitting scrubs that somehow leave a lot and a little to the imagination at the same time.

Dentist comes in. She’s an attractive blond that paid for about 50% of her looks. She looks me full in the face and leans forward.

‘Good news. I can make you a new night guard. You said your last dentist made you a splint?’

‘Yes it worked really well. My jaw never felt better.’

‘Well splints aren’t good because your top teeth need your bottom teeth to strike against. Without that pressure they move around and eventually loosen and fall out.’

‘Oh jeez. Well, it felt great…’

‘I’m sure it did.’ She gives me a pitying smile. Her teeth are so white and her skin is so tan. If you smile while lying in a tanning bed does it bleach your teeth while it’s darkening your skin?

‘Now I have some bad news: you have twelve cavities.’

‘What!? Twelve cavities?’

I am shocked and embarrassed. I put my hand to my mouth. My oral hygiene isn’t that bad, is it? Jesus…I had no idea.

‘How could that be? Two years ago I had none. Do they grow that fast?’

‘They can!’ She brings up the x-ray on the sleek Dell x-ray viewer. ‘See the smudge between these teeth? That’s a cavity.’

I lean forward. ‘I don’t really see it…’

‘Well you can’t because you’re not a dentist. But I can. That’s the worst one. And you have eleven more.’

‘Oh gosh…’

I imagine great painful pits in my teeth, crumbling molars, my grandfather’s champing gums.

‘The good news is I can fill five of them today.’

‘Shoot, I would but I have to get back to work. I’ll reschedule.’

‘Well do it soon. There’s no cure for a cavity you know, and they’ll just get worse!’

Back at work I tell the guys the shocking news and urge them all to brush more often.

‘Wait,’ says Petey. ‘You said you went to Dr. Greene?’ Petey’s a quiet young Mormon guy, but now he gets heated.

‘That freaking dentist…she is the worst, the absolute worst. She said I had fifteen cavities! I was so darn scared. I had her fill the first few but she drilled too deep and I got an abscess and almost freaking died. Whatever you do, don’t go back to her. She’s just out to milk her patients. How do you think she affords that nice office?’

‘It was a nice office…’

‘Plus they give people discounts if they leave a 5-star review.’

‘Oh yeah…they had like 200 reviews and an exactly 5 star rating. That’s sketchy.’

‘Yeah man. Here’s the number to Dr. Frank, the dentist that fixed me.’

***

Dr. Frank’s office has a low drop ceiling with yellowing panels, peeling wallpaper, stacks of files along the back wall, busted-ass waiting room chairs. The fax machine is running loud and hot in the corner. The woman at the desk has normal, baggy scrubs. She calls me ‘hun’.

Dr. Frank is a wide man with a confident grip and a straightforward manner that lives up to his name.

‘I reviewed those x-rays from Dr. Greene. Let’s just say I’m not a fan of her work. She showed you these shadows right? Well I like to call that “trolling for dollars”. They may be cavities. They may not be. It will be years before we can say for sure.’

‘So I don’t have twelve cavities?’

‘Well some of them probably will turn into cavities some day. But not now. And some may just go away.’

‘Really? Because she said—’

‘Oh yeah, I’ve seen it happen. Look, if you were my kid I’d say don’t go drilling anything right now. Don’t let her scare you into doing something you don’t need to do.’

I’m 26, living in Burbank, California. Back in a dental chair with my mouth open. The place isn’t exactly dingy, but it isn’t exactly nice either. I’ve learned my lesson about nice offices. The waiting couch sags, the receptionist reminds me of my second-grade teacher and the hygienist has such muscular forearms that I wonder if she’s there to restrain patients as well as clean their teeth.

Dr. Hong is calling numbers out from inside my mouth to the hygienist who types them into a chunky old Lenovo laptop. Dr. Hong snaps off the yellowing overhead light and gives an exasperated sigh.

‘You need wear night guard. Your teeth terrible. Grinding and clenching all night.’

Damn it. I never got a new one.

‘Hahhyeah I han hegetha nother un hut eely herk?’

He takes the dam out of my mouth and hand-cranks the chair upright.

‘Yes night guard work. But only if you wear it.’

‘But—’

He waves me silent and drops his bombshell.

‘You have to wear night guard. You have teeth of 50-year-old!’

‘What?! The teeth of a 50-year-old!?’

I’m shocked and embarrassed. I run my tongue along the inside of my molars. I mean, I knew I should be wearing the night guard but, god… I had no idea I did such damage.

‘Oh yes, you have old teeth. Very terrible. But night guard only $250. I can take impressions for it today.’

‘But they’re hard to keep in all the time. And there’s my jaw...’

‘Too bad. You need to get used to it. If you my grandson I tell you wear it or you lose your teeth! And hurry up because I retire soon. I will refer you to TMJ guy for jaw.’

‘OK…let’s do it.’

I’m so cowed he could have charged me $1,000 and I still would have paid.

The night guard does not help my jaw. And it pushes a couple teeth out of line so now they strike wrong. Dr. Hong retired and I’m moving soon. I don’t have time to get it adjusted. Plus, is it really doing anything? I don’t think I’m really grinding. It was that stupid tooth reshaping when I was 17…

Eventually I get in with the TMJ specialist, and he refers me to an oral surgeon. ‘Best guy in town for a jaw like yours.’

It seems this surgeon is dental royalty because his dad founded the big university dental school. Junior is a hotshot surgeon but he’s retiring soon so I should get in with him as soon as I can.

I arrive at the swanky building off Wilshire Blvd. Elevator to the 30th floor. Doors open right into the office and I’m greeted by a bored, curvy little blonde with light brown eyes that flash up from her Apple laptop. She instantly catalogs me from under her elegant mascara. No ring. But it’s clear from the wince she passes off as a smile that I wouldn’t have a chance anyway. The office is nice in an old money sort of way: stiff leather chairs, thick wool carpet, muted red and white and gold, immaculately clean.

‘Spa water?’

‘Sure, thanks.’

Dentist is a large tanned man with a quarterback’s hands. He doesn’t use them to shake mine. He has pictures of dead African big game as his Macbook Pro screensaver. He touches his gold-rimmed glasses and pulls up my x-rays.

‘You have what we call a large skeletal anomaly. Essentially your face is deformed. The only way — the only way — to solve it is to saw your jaw apart, graft bone, cut off your gums and move the whole thing over fractions of a millimeter with posts and pins and glue made from your own powdered bone.’

A chill runs up my spine.

‘Plus you have some gum recession which we can take care of at the same time. It is a coordinated care plan that involves four different specialists. It takes about 9 months in total. It will cost about $100,000. Maybe $150,000. But I am confident we can probably help you.’

‘But what about—’

‘It is the only way. Nothing else is really worth getting into.’

‘But—’

‘Look, if you want things to keep getting worse, live your life. But if it was me, I’d bite the bullet and get it over with.’

‘In terms of a second opinion, I think his recommendation was way too drastic,’ says my neighborhood strip mall orthodontist. She’s in her early thirties, still paying off her student loans but not trying to pay them off tomorrow. Office is modest and her assistant is a niece with bad skin.

‘I guess there’s a skeletal anomaly but it’s not bad at all. About 6 months with some gentle Invisalign and you’d be all set. Your jaw will not be perfect, but I can promise that you’ll have a better bite.’

This should make me feel better. But all I feel is exasperation.

‘That’s great. But I don’t know what to think. I got him saying $150k and 9 months, and I got you telling me 6 months of light correction. Who do I believe?’

She shrugs. ‘Well, he’s a surgeon. Maybe every mouth looks like a nail he should hammer.’

I wince at the thought.

‘How could I have prevented this?’

‘Oh well you should have gotten braces when you were young. And a palate expander. But after about 21 your bones are hard and set. No changing them unless you do those crazy surgeries he was talking about.’

‘Damn. So just a little Invisalign?’

‘Yep.’

‘Would you need to do any tooth reshaping or anything like that afterwards?’

‘Oh sure. But that’s nothing. Just fractions of a millimeter. I can take your impressions today if you want to get started?’

‘No thanks. I need to think about it.’

I’m 33, just moved back home to Austin. I never got the Invisalign. Jaw still hurts from time to time. I haven’t had a cleaning in two years. And my tooth sensitivity from the gum recession is getting worse. I can’t drink cold water without pain. My teeth aren’t as sharp as they used to be either. I have not been wearing a night guard. Both my parents have recently gotten root canals and explained the process in graphic detail. They wish they had taken better care of their teeth.

It is time to get my shit together. But first I need to find a good dentist.

‘You should see mine,’ says my sister over tacos. ‘She’s cool and pretty. I call her Hottie Doc. It’s a super nice office.’

‘Hottie Doc? Nice office? No thank you.’

‘Oh trust me, I understand, but they really do good work and they don’t try to upsell you on shit all the time.’

She would know. She was a hygienist after all.

‘OK, well I don’t have any other recommendations and I don’t trust Google so… I guess I’ll give them a shot.’

Spa water. Beautiful hygienist. Cold office. New handheld x-ray machine. Form-fitting scrubs.

‘Well you have 6 cavities,’ says Hottie Doc. Her perfectly bronzed skin glows in the afternoon sun coming in through the floor to ceiling window. ‘See these shadows between the teeth?’

At least I see the shadows now, because they’re bigger. And those were some of the same teeth Dr. Greene said I had cavities in ten years ago. It’s time.

‘OK fine. And what about the gum recession?’

‘Yeah your recession is pretty bad. For that I’ll get you in with the periodontist. It's worth a consult and he’s great.’

‘And the jaw thing?’

‘Well you need a night guard for sure. I’ll make you something called a splint.’

‘Oh no, I’ve tried those before and another dentist said—’

‘Well, you’re not meant to wear them for a long time. A few weeks to allow your jaw to relax so we can see where it wants to go. Then we get you a proper night guard made in that shape, so all night your jaw is relaxed and happy. Your bite will feel off but in the morning it will just go back to where it normally does when you chew.’

‘OK, I guess that makes sense.’

‘And then we’ll refer you to the best ortho in town, Dr. Trudy. She’ll tell you what you need. Are you ready to take care of these cavities? I can do your left side today.’

‘Sure, better now than later right? But god I hate getting my teeth drilled! Every few years I read some promising article about how scientists are working on lab-grown organs and stuff. It’s always like 10 years away from actually being ready. When are we going to be able to just regrow teeth in the lab from our own stem cells or something?’

She guffaws. ‘I don’t know! Ask Elon Musk! OK now lean back and open your mouth.’

Poor form. A good dentist should have more professional curiosity than this. Further thoughts are drowned out by the scream of the dental drill.

On the way out the pretty little hygienist hands me two referrals. She seems too young for how much cleavage her scrubs are showing.

‘This one is for Dr. Trudy the ortho. She is just the best. That’s who my parents took me to.’ Her teeth are wide and white and straight. She has no skeletal anomaly. ‘And here is the referral to the periodontist Dr. Gupta.’

‘Thanks,’ I slur through Novocaine lips. ‘Guess I shouldn’t have been brushing so hard all these years.’

‘Oh that’s been totally disproven as a cause of recession,’ says Hottie Doc, appearing behind the counter. ‘It's caused by grinding and by genetics. Brush as hard as you want. I’ve seen gums grow back after wearing a good night guard.’

‘Oh really? I thought that once gum tissue was gone it was gone forever.’

She shrugs. ‘I’ve seen it. Bye bye now. See you next week for the other side!’

‘Yes, you have some light recession,’ says the periodontist Dr. Gupta. He pops in a mint and sits down onto a fancy swivel chair. Unlike other dentists, Dr. Gupta came by his dark complexion the old-fashioned way. His office is nice but I’m not sure if the same rule about niceness applies to a gum specialist.

‘It’s really not too bad. See all this tissue here? I’d say you’re fine.’

‘Well, that’s good to hear.’

‘The main thing is to manage the sensitivity and not brush too hard.’

‘Wait, I thought hard brushing was disproven?’

‘Not really. Who told you that?’

I feel a surge of anger. Good lord. Do any of these dentists actually know what they’re doing?

‘OK, well I’m getting this night guard which my dentist says will help with the recession.’ He gives a noncommittal head bobble. ‘I’m pretty excited about it because she’s making one that will help my jaw go back to where it wants to be.’

He frowns and squints at my jaw. ‘Hmm, yes. Look, just make sure it’s a flat one, and doesn’t pull your jaw out of alignment. Those sideways ones might feel good while you’re sleeping but then your teeth don’t fit together right. If it's off by fractions of a millimeter you could end up doing serious damage to your teeth and maybe worsening the recession.’

‘Oh. Well I already paid for it. I was really going to do it right this time…’

‘Well if I was your father, I’d say stay away from those types of night guards.’

‘Oh…’

‘As for the recession, if the sensitivity is really bothering you we can do a gum graft. That’s where I scrape tissue off the roof of your mouth, cut into your gums so they lift up in flaps, and then I paint the scraped tissue back on around your teeth and reattach your gums. It costs about $10,000.’

A shiver shoots up my spine.

‘Oh boy. Isn’t that just a stopgap though? Without really knowing what caused it, how do I know the recession won’t keep getting worse?’

‘We don’t. You know, if I were you, I would wait. We’re only a few years away from being able to culture gum tissue from your own stem cells and reapply it painlessly to your teeth.’

‘Really?! Now that’s what I like to hear! And who knows, maybe with light brushing and wearing the night guard, some of it will grow back on its own.’

Dr. Gupta scoffs. ‘That’s a myth. Once gum tissue is gone, it’s gone forever. Who told you that?’

‘My dentist…’

He chuckles. ‘Well, she’s not a perio.’

I catch the unmistakable odor of stale tobacco under the mint on his breath. I notice the outline of a pack of smokes in his scrubs pocket. For Christ’s sake, isn’t smoking a major cause of gum recession?

‘One last question. I saw Dr. Trudy for ortho before I came to you. If I do get the gum treatment, she said I should do the ortho first. Is that right?’

‘Oh, no no no! You do perio first and then the ortho. Moving your teeth around, even fractions of a millimeter without gum coverage, is a good way to lose even more. Listen, Dr. Trudy is…well, let’s just say I am not a fan of her work.’

‘You aren’t?’ I ask weakly. A gray swirl of frustration and confusion and hopelessness wells up inside me.

‘No. In fact, I’m glad she’s retiring. You know, I’ve seen a few cases like yours over the years.’

‘You have?’

‘Yes and with coordinated care, we could really correct your entire mouth. But the first thing you need to do is see an oral surgeon.’

He spins on the little chair and calls to the tall, raven-haired stunner at the front desk.

‘Hey Crystal, who was that really good oral surgeon out in California?’

blocks.x: I’m 17 and my jaw has been hurting, right at the hinge on the right side.

My mom has crowded teeth. My dad has gaps. I must have gotten a little of both because my teeth are straight and even. Good thing, because I’m in high school and braces would dissolve what small nuggets of game I have.
‘Well!’ declares the dentist as he emerges from my mouth. He pulls off his glove and I close my jaw. There’s a pop that could have come from either.

‘The thing is that the two halves of your face didn’t grow at the same rate. Here, take a look.’ He holds up a mirror and I see my disfiguration for the first time. The right side of my jaw is a little crooked. My nose on that side is angled, my eyelid is a slightly different shape.
‘Oh wow…’
I am shocked and embarrassed. I touch my face. I had no idea.
‘So, do I need braces?’

‘No, but your bite is a bit off. Fractions of a millimeter here and there.’ His own teeth strobe out from between his lips as he talks. They rival the overhead lamp for xenon brilliance, accentuated by his deeply tanned skin.
‘You’ll want to get it corrected or you could end up wearing your teeth down. I can do it today if you’re up for it?’
‘I’m not sure…what about my jaw?’
‘Oh it will make that better actually. Your jaw will slot right into place after this. No more sliding around to find the right bite.’
‘Are you sure? Because I really don’t—’
‘If you were my son, I would say the same thing.’
‘OK,’ I say, ‘Let’s do it.’

Tooth reshaping was a euphemism. Voluntary torture would have been more accurate. My teeth fit together better alright. But they are shorter now, and that makes the impingement of my jaw into the right socket worse.
Fucking guy. Never going there again. That hygienist was pretty though…mom-pretty, but still.
I wish I had never done it. But hey, at least I didn’t have to get braces.

I’m 20, in Florida. My face is still warm from the radiation bath the ancient x-ray machine gave me. It is a tall, forbidding machine that would have at least a dozen skulls painted on its nose cone if it was a fighter plane. The office is a couple rooms in an office building basement. The hygienist is out for a back surgery and the front desk lady is sick. So the sweaty old dentist is doing it all himself today.
‘Well no cavities,’ he murmurs, looking at the pictures. The good news momentarily lifts the weary folds at the edge of his mouth but the smile does not reach his sad eyes.
‘Great,’ I say. I expected no less. I am 20 after all, and I will live forever.
‘But looks like you’ve started to grind your teeth. And you say the jaw hurts?’
‘Grind my teeth? I don’t think so.’ I run my tongue along the inside of my teeth.
‘Well, it happens when you’re asleep so you don’t notice.’
Yeah whatever pal.

‘OK. Let’s do it.’
I’m 22, and living in Utah. The splint was great but I’ve lost it and I haven’t had a cleaning in two years. I looked up the top-rated dentist on Google and now I’m walking into my appointment.

I open the door and squint into the shining plasticky sleekness. ‘Hello and welcome!’ beams a beautiful girl with flowing blonde hair and red lips. She sits in a Herman Miller chair behind a white marble countertop. The lights are bright and fancy green wallpaper accents one wall. The office air is chilly, fancy chilly, the kind of chilly that says ‘we don’t care how much electricity costs, as long as you’re comfortable.’
‘Spa water?’
‘Oh wow, sure, thanks.’

The hygienist that does my cleaning is also beautiful, about my age. Ring on though…my sister was a hygienist for a while and wore a fake ring to keep the men at bay. 22 and married? This is Utah, so probably legit.
When did they start cutting scrubs to make them sexy?
Another girl takes my x-rays on a new machine the size of a small ottoman. She also wears form-fitting scrubs that somehow leave a lot and a little to the imagination at the same time.
Dentist comes in. She’s an attractive blond that paid for about 50% of her looks. She looks me full in the face and leans forward.
‘Good news. I can make you a new night guard. You said your last dentist made you a splint?’
‘Yes it worked really well. My jaw never felt better.’
‘Well splints aren’t good because your top teeth need your bottom teeth to strike against. Without that pressure they move around and eventually loosen and fall out.’
‘Oh jeez. Well, it felt great…’
‘I’m sure it did.’ She gives me a pitying smile. Her teeth are so white and her skin is so tan. If you smile while lying in a tanning bed does it bleach your teeth while it’s darkening your skin?
‘Now I have some bad news: you have twelve cavities.’
‘What!? Twelve cavities?’
I am shocked and embarrassed. I put my hand to my mouth. My oral hygiene isn’t that bad, is it? Jesus…I had no idea.
‘How could that be? Two years ago I had none. Do they grow that fast?’
‘They can!’ She brings up the x-ray on the sleek Dell x-ray viewer. ‘See the smudge between these teeth? That’s a cavity.’
I lean forward. ‘I don’t really see it…’

I imagine great painful pits in my teeth, crumbling molars, my grandfather’s champing gums.
‘The good news is I can fill five of them today.’
‘Shoot, I would but I have to get back to work. I’ll reschedule.’
‘Well do it soon. There’s no cure for a cavity you know, and they’ll just get worse!’
Back at work I tell the guys the shocking news and urge them all to brush more often.
‘Wait,’ says Petey. ‘You said you went to Dr. Greene?’ Petey’s a quiet young Mormon guy, but now he gets heated.

‘That freaking dentist…she is the worst, the absolute worst. She said I had fifteen cavities! I was so darn scared. I had her fill the first few but she drilled too deep and I got an abscess and almost freaking died. Whatever you do, don’t go back to her. She’s just out to milk her patients. ‘It was a nice office…’
‘Plus they give people discounts if they leave a 5-star review.’
‘Oh yeah…they had like 200 reviews and an exactly 5 star rating. That’s sketchy.’
‘Yeah man. Here’s the number to Dr. Frank, the dentist that fixed me.’

Dr. Frank’s office has a low drop ceiling with yellowing panels, peeling wallpaper, stacks of files along the back wall, busted-ass waiting room chairs. The fax machine is running loud and hot in the corner. The woman at the desk has normal, baggy scrubs. She calls me ‘hun’.
Dr. Frank is a wide man with a confident grip and a straightforward manner that lives up to his name.

‘I reviewed those x-rays from Dr. Greene. Let’s just say I’m not a fan of her work. She showed you these shadows right? Well I like to call that “trolling for dollars”. They may be cavities. They may not be. It will be years before we can say for sure.’
‘So I don’t have twelve cavities?’
‘Well some of them probably will turn into cavities some day. But not now. And some may just go away.’
‘Really? Because she said—’
‘Oh yeah, I’ve seen it happen. Look, if you were my kid I’d say don’t go drilling anything right now. Don’t let her scare you into doing something you don’t need to do.’

Dr. Hong is calling numbers out from inside my mouth to the hygienist who types them into a chunky old Lenovo laptop. Dr. Hong snaps off the yellowing overhead light and gives an exasperated sigh.
‘You need wear night guard. Your teeth terrible. Grinding and clenching all night.’
