‘Yes, you have some light recession,’ says the periodontist Dr. Gupta. He pops in a mint and sits down onto a fancy swivel chair. Unlike other dentists, Dr. Gupta came by his dark complexion the old-fashioned way. His office is nice but I’m not sure if the same rule about niceness applies to a gum specialist.
‘It’s really not too bad. See all this tissue here? I’d say you’re fine.’
‘Well, that’s good to hear.’
‘The main thing is to manage the sensitivity and not brush too hard.’
‘Wait, I thought hard brushing was disproven?’

https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!0ZJb!,w_32,h_32,c_fill,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8ca8c6a2-8527-403a-b730-3cb6ca1407c0_144x144.png
‘Not really. Who told you that?’
I feel a surge of anger. Good lord. Do any of these dentists actually know what they’re doing?

‘OK, well I’m getting this night guard which my dentist says will help with the recession.’ He gives a noncommittal head bobble. ‘I’m pretty excited about it because she’s making one that will help my jaw go back to where it wants to be.’

He frowns and squints at my jaw. ‘Hmm, yes. Look, just make sure it’s a flat one, and doesn’t pull your jaw out of alignment. Those sideways ones might feel good while you’re sleeping but then your teeth don’t fit together right. If it's off by fractions of a millimeter you could end up doing serious damage to your teeth and maybe worsening the recession.’
‘Oh. Well I already paid for it. I was really going to do it right this time…’
‘Well if I was your father, I’d say stay away from those types of night guards.’
‘Oh…’

‘As for the recession, if the sensitivity is really bothering you we can do a gum graft. That’s where I scrape tissue off the roof of your mouth, cut into your gums so they lift up in flaps, and then I paint the scraped tissue back on around your teeth and reattach your gums. It costs about $10,000.’
A shiver shoots up my spine.
‘Oh boy. Isn’t that just a stopgap though? Without really knowing what caused it, how do I know the recession won’t keep getting worse?’
‘We don’t. You know, if I were you, I would wait. We’re only a few years away from being able to culture gum tissue from your own stem cells and reapply it painlessly to your teeth.’
‘Really?! Now that’s what I like to hear! And who knows, maybe with light brushing and wearing the night guard, some of it will grow back on its own.’
Dr. Gupta scoffs. ‘That’s a myth. Once gum tissue is gone, it’s gone forever. Who told you that?’
‘My dentist…’
He chuckles. ‘Well, she’s not a perio.’

I catch the unmistakable odor of stale tobacco under the mint on his breath. I notice the outline of a pack of smokes in his scrubs pocket. For Christ’s sake, isn’t smoking a major cause of gum recession?
‘One last question. I saw Dr. Trudy for ortho before I came to you. If I do get the gum treatment, she said I should do the ortho first. Is that right?’

‘Oh, no no no! You do perio first and then the ortho. Moving your teeth around, even fractions of a millimeter without gum coverage, is a good way to lose even more. Listen, Dr. Trudy is…well, let’s just say I am not a fan of her work.’
‘You aren’t?’ I ask weakly. A gray swirl of frustration and confusion and hopelessness wells up inside me.
‘No. In fact, I’m glad she’s retiring. You know, I’ve seen a few cases like yours over the years.’
‘You have?’
‘Yes and with coordinated care, we could really correct your entire mouth. But the first thing you need to do is see an oral surgeon.’
He spins on the little chair and calls to the tall, raven-haired stunner at the front desk.
‘Hey Crystal, who was that really good oral surgeon out in California?’

items.title: Americans' social activity has steeply declined in the past 30 years
items.author: hubraumhugo
items.summary: In recent years, there has been extensive discussion of a social decline in the United States, including a U.S. surgeon general advisory in 2023 that declared
items.text:
In recent years, there has been extensive discussion of a social decline in the United States, including a U.S. surgeon general advisory in 2023 that declared American loneliness to be an “epidemic.”

Various surveys have tracked America’s social decline over the past few decades. Tracking data from the American Time Use Survey shows that Americans are spending more time alone and less time with friends than they were two decades ago. Perhaps most notably, the American Perspectives Survey has found that from 1990 to 2021, the percentage of Americans with five or more close friends dropped by 25 points, from 63% to 38%.

But while extensive public tracking data show general declines in Americans’ socialization, little, if any, public data show what this looks like for the average American — how the day-to-day activities Americans participate in have changed over the past few decades.

In a new survey, Data for Progress surveyed 1,098 U.S. adults and asked them how many times they engaged in various specific social activities in the past 12 months. These questions directly replicate the DDB Needham Life Style surveys, which tracked Americans’ participation in various activities from 1975-1999 and were referenced in Robert Putnam’s 2000 book “Bowling Alone.” In this analysis, Data for Progress’ 2026 data is compared with the DDB Needham Life Style survey from 1995, which is the earliest year in which full data for all comparison questions was available.

This survey finds significant, double-digit declines in Americans’ participation in key social activities from 1995 to 2026.

The chart below compares the percentage of Americans who report participating in each tested activity at least one time in the past 12 months, between the 1995 and 2026 surveys. We find that Americans’ participation in various social activities has declined by double-digit margins, including attending a class or seminar (-22), entertaining people in your home (-21), attending church or a place of worship (-20), going on a picnic (-19), going to a club meeting (-19), playing cards (-19), going out to breakfast at a restaurant (-13), and doing volunteer work (-12).

A few activities have seen increased engagement: using the internet (+90), playing a home video game (+22), attending an exercise class (+14), going to a pop or rock concert (+13), and taking an airline trip for personal reasons (+5).

Methodology note: This analysis compares two surveys conducted using different methodologies, including differences in constructing sampling frames, modes, and weighting approaches. The findings below should be read as suggestive of trends, not a precise estimate of change. Please see the “Methodology” section below for more information.

One of the steepest declines in the survey is for “entertaining people in my home.” While in 1995, 88% of Americans reported entertaining others at home at least once in the past year, this number has declined to 67% in 2026.

Church attendance has dropped from 74% in 1995 to 54% in 2026.

The percentage of Americans who report having gone on a picnic in the past year has declined from 58% in 1995 to 39% in 2026.

There has also been a 19-point decline in attendance at club meetings, from 45% in 1995 to 26% in 2026.

This analysis adds to existing public data on America’s social decline. Previous reports have found that Americans are spending less time with others and reporting fewer close friends. This new analysis demonstrates that Americans are indeed spending less time in specific social settings, such as restaurants, churches, picnics, parties, bars, and social clubs.

Methodology

The DDB Needham survey was conducted by Market Facts using a stratified quota sampling procedure that begins with a sampling frame acquired from commercial list brokers. The sample oversamples by demographics such as race, gender, and marital status to oversample lower propensity respondents. Finally, the survey contacted individuals via mail.

In comparison, the Data for Progress adult sample was conducted through web panel suppliers and ensured national representativeness via quota fielding and post-stratification weighting.

There is plenty of research on the compositional differences that exist across survey collection modes, and this is likely to affect these results as questions about religiosity and loneliness tend to demonstrate modal differences and social desirability biases. We understand that these factors are at play in our comparison, but find that the magnitude and consistency in trends across measures is a substantial signal about trends in behaviors nonetheless.

items.title: We’re releasing Jev 1.14.0 along with experimental features for dreamers
items.author: emschwartz
items.summary: TL;DR: We're releasing an improved Jev 1.14.0 along with experimental features for our dreamers: images, a new type, and longer context. Enter the danger zone
items.text:
TL;DR: We're releasing an improved Jev 1.14.0 along with experimental features for our dreamers: images, a new type, and longer context. Enter the danger zone at your own risk. 🔥

Our philosophy

A huge debate we’ve been having is on the balance between reliability and creativity.

To really care about the prod builders, we should be shipping models that meet our quality bar for intelligence and have been battle-tested to the limits of what we can do internally.

On the other hand, there’s no way that our team has a full understanding of what is needed to spark delight in the world and build sick sci-fi. We don’t want to impose our values of extreme reliability on those dreamers.

Our solution: share those dreamer-ready features under “danger zone” flags in our API headers. These are features that will be here to stay for future models, are (as far as we can tell) better than what exists out there, and will continue to get better by leaps and bounds. But as a warning, we think there is still way too much jaggedness for us to vouch for these for production use cases!

See these new capabilities as a continuation of what we’ve built over 2 years of stealth. They’re less ready for automation, but very fun to play with. They’re also an early glimpse into what we’re focused on making reliable enough to meet TypeSafe standards.

Composable Images

Not only are we enabling multimodality for future Jev models, we’re enabling it for the current Jev that you all know and love. Surprise: the Jev you all know and love (jev-1.13.0) was multimodal all along!

Image support is fully composable via a find-and-replace in assets. You can put them anywhere that our JSON interface supports: in the state, instructions, or even criteria! Play around with it, push the boundaries of technology, and let us know where Jev can improve.

As a warning, all models (Jev included) perform worse on multimodality over pure text. Breaking down questions into the simplest possible decompositions helps a lot.

TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images: true

Check out docs: docs.typesafe.ai/go/images

Types Beyond Decisions

We’re introducing another new type as well: box. It returns a single bounding box - no type errors allowed. It’s our first type that’s not purely meant for smart-if statements, and is a preview for our explorations beyond simple decisions into what else System One Models can support.

We made huge leaps and bounds on this one recently, so we’re enabling this only for jev-1.14.0 (spoilers).

Check out docs: docs.typesafe.ai/go/box

Size does matter, apparently 💅

We’ve heard you loud and clear on context lengths. Jev actually supports a much longer context length than we’ve enabled in production. We chose to limit it intentionally because Jev, like all models, is less reliable on longer contexts, and this constraint encourages more effective usage patterns in prod.

We aren’t your parents though, so while we strongly recommend limiting context length, you no longer have to:

TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Long-Context: true

Check out docs: docs.typesafe.ai/models#context-length

Opt-in to help us

We love the community’s desire to help make models better! We’ve added an opt-in to allow you to help find model jaggedness with your queries. We will still not train on your queries, but this does make it easier for us to find issues and help debug your use cases.

jev-1.14.0

We’re also releasing a new version of Jev under jev-preview! Not meant to be flashy but instead be small, subtle improvements to everything. Most things should be a tiny bit better, but we expect the largest gain in multi-lingual support.

Model releases should generally also be strict improvements, but we’re well aware of how much developers hate updating their dependencies. jev-latest will be updated to jev-1.14.0 in a week. jev-1.13.0 will be available for a while.

We intend to give 60 days warning before jev-1.13.0 is formally deprecated, and 30 days for jev-1.14.0. We’ll release a deprecation policy prior to this.

Measuring Intelligence

As you all know, we dislike public benchmarks. However, we have our own internal best guesses on how to measure the form factor of intelligence that matters most for developers.

We’re trying something new out here: we’re going to treat you guys like adults and share this with you all.

Some nuance

This measurement is our best guess and will continue to evolve. If ever we show you our internal numbers again, don’t expect them to be consistent.

Don’t believe it entirely. Always favor your own experimentation and evals with your use cases.

We’re including only open weight models because we guard our validation set very closely and are spooked out about the data policies of our model providers.

This is likely biased towards our models. Feel free to ignore our model, and instead focus on the relative ranking of open source models.

What’s next

Lots of people love to ask what kind of sci-fi we’re releasing next. While we are working on some mindblowing stuff, expect most releases to be beautifully boring (like we think AI should be): small improvements across the board, better stability, and features for real deployment.

items.title: Better HTTP/1 connection reuse in Go 1.27
items.author: allddd
items.text:
Take a look at the following function:

func getStatus(url string) (int, error) {
resp, err := http.Get(url)
if err != nil {
return 0, err
}
defer resp.Body.Close()
return resp.StatusCode, nil
}

It sends a GET request to url and returns the HTTP status code.

Using HTTP/1 (GODEBUG=http2client=0), calling this function 100 times against
index.golang.org takes ~710 milliseconds on Go 1.26
on my machine. On Go 1.27, the same program takes ~150 milliseconds.

That is almost 5 times faster! How is such a drastic performance difference
possible?

The cost of establishing HTTP connections

To understand the difference, consider what happens on the network when we make
an HTTP request.

Go’s net/http package supports HTTP/1.0, HTTP/1.1, and
HTTP/2. All three run over TCP, and usually over TLS when talking to HTTPS
endpoints. Making a request over a new connection looks something like this:

TCP handshake (1 RTT): the client sends a SYN packet, the server
replies with SYN-ACK, and the client replies with ACK. Because the
client can send the first TLS message alongside that final ACK,
establishing the TCP connection takes 1 round-trip time (RTT).

TLS handshake (2 RTT): next, a TLS handshake exchanges encryption keys
and verifies the server’s identity; using TLS 1.2, this takes 2 RTT.

HTTP request: with the keys exchanged, HTTP requests can finally be sent
after a total of 3 RTT.

These round trips (plus some CPU time spent on TLS handshakes) add up quickly.
In cross-region communications, one-way latencies often reach or exceed the 50
ms (100 ms RTT) shown in the diagram above. Compared to the 300 ms spent just
setting up the connection, the HTTP request itself can be cheap to serve, taking
only a little over 1 RTT when bandwidth is plentiful or the HTTP response is
small.

Even in more favorable conditions, opening a new connection can still be
expensive. Our opening benchmark queries
index.golang.org, which is distributed worldwide and
supports TLS 1.3. This means that latency is relatively low, and the TLS
handshake can actually finish in just 1 RTT. Even so, the performance difference
is still very noticeable.

Connection reuse

To avoid paying this setup cost on every request, HTTP clients and servers try
to reuse existing connections across multiple requests when possible. The
mechanics of this differ based on the HTTP version:

HTTP/1.0: while not part of the official specification, clients and
servers often opt into connection reuse by sending a Connection: keep-alive header. Reuse continues until either endpoint omits the header
or sends a Connection: close header.

HTTP/1.1: connections are persistent by default, and can be reused for
subsequent requests and responses unless either side declares otherwise by
sending a Connection: close header.

HTTP/2: multiple requests and responses can be multiplexed over a single
TCP connection.

When connection reuse fails

In HTTP/1 (both HTTP/1.0 and HTTP/1.1), multiple requests and responses on the
same connection are sent sequentially on the wire. If two GET requests are
sent to index.golang.org over the same TCP
connection, the responses arrive as a single stream of bytes:

As shown in the diagram, net/http.Get reads and parses
the status line and headers from the byte stream to populate
net/http.Response, then returns immediately. The
response body remains unread on the connection and is consumed only as the
caller reads from net/http.Response.Body.

Because responses are sent back-to-back on the same stream,
net/http can only find the start of the next response after
the current response body has been read to the very end (as determined by the
Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding header).

Now look back at our example program, where we never read resp.Body:

func getStatus(url string) (int, error) {
resp, err := http.Get(url)
if err != nil {
return 0, err
}
defer resp.Body.Close()
return resp.StatusCode, nil
}

Through Go 1.26, when resp.Body.Close is called, net/http
sees that there is still an unread response body. Realizing that it cannot reuse
the connection, it abandons the existing connection and creates new connections
for its next requests, causing it to repeatedly incur the cost of establishing
new connections.

(HTTP/2 does not have this problem. Because it multiplexes streams of frames
over a single connection rather than sending responses strictly back-to-back, an
unread response body on one stream does not block other requests from sharing
the connection.)

Where failed connection reuse hurts

This subtlety of HTTP/1 connection reuse can cause silent performance
degradation in seemingly innocuous code.

As in our opening example, a client might only care about an API response’s
status code. However, the API endpoint it is talking to might send bodies that
provide more detailed but ultimately unused information, such as {"success": true, "message": "update processed"}. This will unfortunately cause connection
reuse to fail.

Even programs that do read the response body can run into this issue if they
stop just short of the end of the body. For example,
encoding/json.Decoder stops reading as soon as
it sees the closing } of a JSON object. If a server sends a JSON response
terminated with a newline, decoding the JSON object will leave the newline still
unread. The connection cannot be reused for a new request until that newline is
consumed. Thus, a healthy connection might end up being abandoned, even though
it was only a single byte away from being reusable.

The manual solution

The unread body problem has been a long-standing sharp edge. Over the years,
many Go developers came up with their own workarounds. Most commonly, this is
done by draining the response body prior to closing it:

func getStatus(url string) (int, error) {
resp, err := http.Get(url)
if err != nil {
return 0, err
}
drainAndCloseBody(resp.Body)
return resp.StatusCode, nil
}
func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) {
io.Copy(io.Discard, body) // Drain the response body before closing it.
body.Close()
}

While this works for small responses, if the unread body is large, establishing
a new TCP connection can be faster than downloading and discarding the rest of
the body. A better approach is to cap the number of bytes we are willing to
drain:

func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) {
io.CopyN(io.Discard, body, 256<<10) // Only drain up to 256 KB.
body.Close()
}

However, a server might send a response body that trickles in slowly, so we also
need to cap the time we spend draining:

func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) {
drainDone := make(chan struct{}, 1)
go func() {
io.CopyN(io.Discard, body, 256<<10) // Only drain up to 256 KB.
drainDone <- struct{}{}
}()
// Only spend at most 50 ms trying to drain the response body.
select {
case <-drainDone:
case <-time.After(50 * time.Millisecond):
// If we reach the 50 ms timeout, body.Close will run and interrupt the
// io.CopyN, preventing goroutine leaks.
}
body.Close()
}

Of course, we also do not want to block for up to 50 milliseconds when closing a
response body. Instead, we can drain the body asynchronously in the background
and let it race against subsequent requests:

func drainAndCloseBody(body io.ReadCloser) {
drainDone := make(chan struct{}, 1)
go func() {
io.CopyN(io.Discard, body, 256<<10) // Only drain up to 256 KB.
drainDone <- struct{}{}
}()
go func() {
// Only spend at most 50 ms trying to drain the response body.
select {
case <-drainDone:
// If the drain can finish before a new request is sent, the
// connection will be reused; otherwise, a new connection is
// created, and the current connection will be put in a pool of
// idle connections, potentially being reused for another future
// request.
case <-time.After(50 * time.Millisecond):
// If we reach the 50 ms timeout, body.Close will run and interrupt
// the io.CopyN, preventing goroutine leaks.
}
body.Close()
}()
}

As we can see, draining response bodies safely is surprisingly tricky and
cumbersome. Worse, as the practice of draining response bodies spread, some
nuances were often lost. This has led to misunderstandings such as attempting to
drain response bodies for HTTP/2 connections, when doing so is unnecessary.

The current state and conclusion

Starting in Go 1.27, net/http.Transport
automatically does everything we have implemented in the code above: it will
asynchronously drain an unread HTTP/1 response body for up to 50 ms or 256 KB.
It also implements additional optimizations; for example, when a response
contains the Connection: close header, draining the body is guaranteed to be
wasted work, and it therefore skips doing so. Note that this behavior might
evolve in future versions of Go, as other possible enhancements become apparent.

As a general best practice, we now recommend that users simply close their HTTP
bodies once they no longer need them, like in our original example:

func getStatus(url string) (int, error) {
resp, err := http.Get(url)
if err != nil {
return 0, err
}
defer resp.Body.Close()
return resp.StatusCode, nil
}

Go is all about simplicity. Let your code stay clean and simple, and let
net/http deal with the complexities on your behalf.

blocks.x: Take a look at the following function:
It sends a GET request to url and returns the HTTP status code.

Using HTTP/1 (GODEBUG=http2client=0), calling this function 100 times against
index.golang.org takes ~710 milliseconds on Go 1.26
on my machine. On Go 1.27, the same program takes ~150 milliseconds.

That is almost 5 times faster! How is such a drastic performance difference
possible?
The cost of establishing HTTP connections

To understand the difference, consider what happens on the network when we make
an HTTP request.

Go’s net/http package supports HTTP/1.0, HTTP/1.1, and
HTTP/2. All three run over TCP, and usually over TLS when talking to HTTPS
endpoints. Making a request over a new connection looks something like this:

TCP handshake (1 RTT): the client sends a SYN packet, the server
replies with SYN-ACK, and the client replies with ACK. Because the
client can send the first TLS message alongside that final ACK,
establishing the TCP connection takes 1 round-trip time (RTT).

TLS handshake (2 RTT): next, a TLS handshake exchanges encryption keys
and verifies the server’s identity; using TLS 1.2, this takes 2 RTT.

HTTP request: with the keys exchanged, HTTP requests can finally be sent
after a total of 3 RTT.

These round trips (plus some CPU time spent on TLS handshakes) add up quickly.
In cross-region communications, one-way latencies often reach or exceed the 50
ms (100 ms RTT) shown in the diagram above. Compared to the 300 ms spent just
setting up the connection, the HTTP request itself can be cheap to serve, taking
only a little over 1 RTT when bandwidth is plentiful or the HTTP response is
small.

Even in more favorable conditions, opening a new connection can still be
expensive. Our opening benchmark queries
index.golang.org, which is distributed worldwide and
supports TLS 1.3. This means that latency is relatively low, and the TLS
handshake can actually finish in just 1 RTT. Even so, the performance difference
is still very noticeable.
Connection reuse

To avoid paying this setup cost on every request, HTTP clients and servers try
to reuse existing connections across multiple requests when possible. The
mechanics of this differ based on the HTTP version:

HTTP/1.0: while not part of the official specification, clients and
servers often opt into connection reuse by sending a Connection: keep-alive header. Reuse continues until either endpoint omits the header
or sends a Connection: close header.

HTTP/1.1: connections are persistent by default, and can be reused for
subsequent requests and responses unless either side declares otherwise by
sending a Connection: close header.

HTTP/2: multiple requests and responses can be multiplexed over a single
TCP connection.
When connection reuse fails

In HTTP/1 (both HTTP/1.0 and HTTP/1.1), multiple requests and responses on the
same connection are sent sequentially on the wire. If two GET requests are
sent to index.golang.org over the same TCP
connection, the responses arrive as a single stream of bytes:

As shown in the diagram, net/http.Get reads and parses
the status line and headers from the byte stream to populate
net/http.Response, then returns immediately. The
response body remains unread on the connection and is consumed only as the
caller reads from net/http.Response.Body.

Because responses are sent back-to-back on the same stream,
net/http can only find the start of the next response after
the current response body has been read to the very end (as determined by the
Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding header).
Now look back at our example program, where we never read resp.Body:

Through Go 1.26, when resp.Body.Close is called, net/http
sees that there is still an unread response body. Realizing that it cannot reuse
the connection, it abandons the existing connection and creates new connections
for its next requests, causing it to repeatedly incur the cost of establishing
new connections.

(HTTP/2 does not have this problem. Because it multiplexes streams of frames
over a single connection rather than sending responses strictly back-to-back, an
unread response body on one stream does not block other requests from sharing
the connection.)
Where failed connection reuse hurts

This subtlety of HTTP/1 connection reuse can cause silent performance
degradation in seemingly innocuous code.

As in our opening example, a client might only care about an API response’s
status code. However, the API endpoint it is talking to might send bodies that
provide more detailed but ultimately unused information, such as {"success": true, "message": "update processed"}. This will unfortunately cause connection
reuse to fail.

Even programs that do read the response body can run into this issue if they
stop just short of the end of the body. For example,
encoding/json.Decoder stops reading as soon as
it sees the closing } of a JSON object. If a server sends a JSON response
terminated with a newline, decoding the JSON object will leave the newline still
unread. The connection cannot be reused for a new request until that newline is
consumed. Thus, a healthy connection might end up being abandoned, even though
it was only a single byte away from being reusable.
The manual solution

The unread body problem has been a long-standing sharp edge. Over the years,
many Go developers came up with their own workarounds. Most commonly, this is
done by draining the response body prior to closing it:

While this works for small responses, if the unread body is large, establishing
a new TCP connection can be faster than downloading and discarding the rest of
the body. A better approach is to cap the number of bytes we are willing to
drain:

However, a server might send a response body that trickles in slowly, so we also
need to cap the time we spend draining:

Of course, we also do not want to block for up to 50 milliseconds when closing a
response body. Instead, we can drain the body asynchronously in the background
and let it race against subsequent requests:

As we can see, draining response bodies safely is surprisingly tricky and

items.title: LFM2.5-24B-A2B: Built for fast on-device agents
items.author: gmays
items.summary: Today, we release LFM2.5-24B-A2B, a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It is the largest
items.text:
Today, we release LFM2.5-24B-A2B, a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It is the largest and final model in the LFM2.5 family, which now spans two orders of magnitude: from LFM2.5-230M to LFM2.5-24B-A2B.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is competitive with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, a model with ~50% more total and active parameters, on five of eight agentic and tool-use benchmarks, scoring 48.09 on LiveClaw versus 38.19 and 27.69 on AutomationBench versus 8.72. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, it runs up to 1.7× faster than comparable MoEs on-device, with 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max and up to 21K output tokens/s on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU.

The base (LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base) and post-trained (LFM2.5-24B-A2B) models are open-weight and available today on Hugging Face and our Playground. Check out our docs on how to run and fine-tune it locally.

What changed since LFM2-24B-A2B

LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on our previous LFM2-24B-A2B release, with an expanded vocabulary and context window, scaled-up pretraining, and large-scale reinforcement learning. Unlike its predecessor, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer. We adopted this strategy to leverage its high decode speed and improve answer quality.

Architecture. It keeps the 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The two architectural changes are the context window extension from 32,768 to 131,072 tokens, and the in-place tokenizer expansion, which doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization.

Pre-training was scaled up from 17T tokens to 33T tokens.

Mid-training has two phases. The first runs 2T tokens at 32K context on curated, higher-quality data weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text. The second runs 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases to prepare the model for agentic workloads.

Post-training turns LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base into the agentic LFM2.5-24B-A2B in a five-stage pipeline as illustrated below: (1) Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), (2) Teacher Specialization, (3) non-agentic and (4) agentic Multi-Domain On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and (5) Agentic Reinforcement Learning (Agentic RL), training the model inside agent harnesses, such as OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenCode.

During teacher specialization, LFM2.5-24B-A2B exhibited well-known reward-hacking behaviors: searching for the final answer in a repository's git history or on platforms like GitHub, PyPI, and Hugging Face. More surprisingly, it even figured out it was in a sandbox, as shown in the examples below.

This behavior looks emergent but might be explained by training data containing similar patterns. We tightened our sandboxes in response, and all reported results below come from sealed evaluation environments.

Benchmarks

We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B across 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. Despite being the smallest model in total and active number of parameters, it is competitive with, and often outperforms, larger MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters, such as Qwen3.6-35B-A3B.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), with its widest margin on AutomationBench, where it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode.

The results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B an ideal foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device. For knowledge-heavy workloads, we recommend pairing LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search, which plays to its tool-calling strength.

Fast inference everywhere

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem:

llama.cpp — GGUF checkpoints for efficient edge inference

MLX — Optimized inference for Apple Silicon

vLLM — GPU-accelerated serving for production throughput

SGLang — High-performance GPU serving framework

ONNX — Cross-platform inference across diverse accelerators

All runs were collected on Pipette, the same benchmarking infrastructure behind Liquid AI's public device performance data.

Edge inference. Due to the efficient LFM2 architecture, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs at reading in prompts and generating answers. It decodes 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on an AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395, up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

items.title: Submarine cable resilience
items.author: speckx
items.summary:
JaredMcKenzie, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

The Matsu Islands are an archipelago of 36 islands in the East China Sea, alongside the southeastern coast of
items.text:
JaredMcKenzie, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

The Matsu Islands are an archipelago of 36 islands in the East China Sea, alongside the southeastern coast of mainland China. The islands have been administered since 1949 by Taiwan, part of a larger set of outlying islands administered by Taiwan, which includes the Kinmen and Penghu Islands, which all lie in the Taiwan Strait.

The Matsu Islands are connected to Taiwan’s main island by two submarine cables — Taima No.2, Taima No.3, and soon Taima No.4. The Taiwan Strait is a shallow body of water, with an average depth of 70m. The submarine cables that lie on this seafloor are vulnerable to damage from ship-based activity, like being snagged by fishing equipment or anchors. But these particular cables have been remarkably unlucky. Between 2018 and 2022, the submarine cables between Taiwan and the Matsu Islands were cut 27 times, and there have been four major outages in the three years from 2023 to 2025.

That’s not the only location where submarine cables have suffered many faults. The Baltic Sea is a shallow sea that has a dozen or so submarine communications cables, and undersea electricity and gas pipelines. There have been 11 disruptions to these submarine systems since 2023. Again, a very unlucky track record.

There are an estimated total of 1.5M kilometres of subsea communications cables, used by 607 in-service submarine cable systems (Figure 1) that are critical to the world’s telecommunications services. If they are put out of service for any reason, our satellite systems simply could not replace them. In such a catastrophic scenario, some communities would be totally isolated, with severe logistical and economic ramifications.

We regard this collection of submarine cable systems as critical infrastructure for global communication services, and we take care to make them as resilient as possible. Modern warfare can deliberately disrupt communications systems, which adds another source of potential damage to the list of geological and accidental risks facing subsea cables.

On the night of 4 August 1914, days after Britain declared war against Germany, the British cable ship HMTS Alert sailed from Dover into the English Channel. The vessel dragged grappling hooks along the seabed, hauled up five German transatlantic and European telegraph cables, and cut them. This severed Germany’s direct, secure submarine cable links to the Americas, Africa, Spain, and the rest of Europe. Germany was forced to rely on wireless radio transmissions, where British intelligence could readily eavesdrop. If the German cryptography used to protect these wireless communications was broken, then it allowed the British to track military movements and capture critical messages, such as the Zimmermann Telegram.
This same action to deliberately sever undersea cables was repeated by the British in September 1939, cutting German cables to Lisbon and New York.

Protecting the cable

These thin polyester-coated cables at the bottom of the ocean are vulnerable, including to:

Geology in the form of submarine earthquakes or landslips

Being snagged by dragging ship anchors or fishing equipment along the seafloor

Deliberate attacks on the cables with grapnels and cutting equipment

How can cables defend against such risks? The inner core of the fibre optic cables and its copper conductor sheath can be wrapped in additional layers of steel cable jacketing as a form of armour (Figure 2). This is mostly used to reduce its vulnerability to shipping accidents.

Figure 2 is somewhat misleading. What is depicted here is a cross-section of submarine cable used in the segments of the cable that lead to the surface cable station. The cable segments that are laid on the deep-sea floor use just the inner components: Optical fibre and a single thin steel thread wrapped in a silicone gel, surrounded by a copper sheath (used to power the cable repeaters), and wrapped in polyethylene. There are no external armour elements. These deep-sea cable segments are around 20mm in diameter, or the size of a garden hose.

The cable surfaces at a cable landing station. These landing stations are typically plain, secured facilities with reliable power. The preferred location is a coastal point with a low volume of fishing or other maritime traffic, and a steep rise from the deep-sea floor. Cables are at their greatest risk from coastal shipping activity, so the shorter the distance from the deep-sea floor to the cable station on dry land, the better.

Many jurisdictions also declare ‘Cable Protection Zones’ as a warning to marine vessel operators that there are cables on the seafloor in this area, and ships should refrain from fishing activity and anchoring in these areas.

Cable routing

Cable routing is also important in terms of resilience. There are several objectives in a cable route, and not all of them can be optimized at the same time.

The cable route should be as short as possible, as additional cable length raises capital costs and increases end-to-end signal delay.

Cables should avoid areas of active geological activity where possible, such as tectonic plate boundaries and mid-plate rifts. Deeper is better, but within reason. Cables on the floor of a deep ocean section are less vulnerable to shipping activity and hostile efforts to disrupt the cable, but with extreme depths it’s more challenging to locate and raise the cable when undertaking a repair.

Sometimes there are geographic ‘choke points’ through which many cables are routed. The Bab al-Mandab Strait is not just a choke point for surface vessels passing between the Indian Ocean and the Red Sea, but it is also the conduit through which 16 cables pass (Figure 4). In September 2025, several cables were severed in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, disrupting an estimated 25% of cable capacity between Asia, Europe, and the Middle East. Houthi-controlled waters remain effectively ungovernable for cable protection.

There is also the Singapore Strait, a major junction for 35 cable systems (Figure 5). This is a shallow water strait that also hosts a significant volume of surface shipping.

Further north, between Taiwan and the Philippines is the Luzon Strait, where 18 cables pass (Figure 6). This was the location of an earthquake and a subsequent set of submarine landslides in December 2006 that not only severed all the cables running through this strait, but also buried many of them under deep layers of sediment. It took 11 repair vessels 49 days to bring all the cable systems back into operation.

The Black Sea is an area with geopolitical risk and regulatory gaps. While mine risk is confirmed, no cable faults have been directly documented in the war in Ukraine. Russia’s continued presence and the conflict make this region functionally inaccessible for routine cable maintenance.

Geopolitics also plays a role in cable routing. Cable owners will prefer to avoid routes through politically unstable territorial waters if suitable alternative routes exist. There are also political considerations. If a cable lands in US territory, then the cable is subject to several Federal Communications Commission (FCC) constraints, including banning equipment or services from companies the FCC see as a threat to US national security. The FCC has also refused to permit the landing of a cable on US territory if the cable also lands in a territory that the US deems to be a foreign adversary.

Land routes are avoided in general, but there are some circumstances where a land route is the preferred option. Connectivity between Asia and Europe would normally run through the Bab al-Mandab Strait, landing in Egypt in the Gulf of Suez, then overland through Egypt to get to the Mediterranean Sea. There is an alternative route through the Persian Gulf, Iraq and Türkiye, although this entails a segment that transits the Strait of Hormuz, or a second overland segment through Oman and the United Arab Emirates.

Cable faults

Around 200 submarine cable faults are reported worldwide each year, a figure that the International Cable Protection Committee notes has stayed broadly steady in recent years even as the total cable inventory increases. The cables themselves are remarkably reliable. It is the maritime traffic above them that is the cause of most of the problems. 86% of cable faults are likely due to fishing activity or anchoring, and fishing activity is around twice as prevalent as anchoring incidents.

Geological events, such as submarine landslides and seabed movement, account for about 7% of cable faults, cable abrasion for 4%, and component failure (in repeaters) for only 4%.

With the high correlation of faults and maritime activity, it is not surprising that just under one half of cable faults occur in territorial waters, and most of the remainder occur in exclusive economic zones. Just 2% occur on the high seas. Cables are most vulnerable close to shore, in shallow water, where fishing is concentrated, where ships anchor, and where the cable must come ashore at a landing station alongside every other cable serving that coast. The deep ocean, where there is little seabed fishing activity and few ships anchoring, is the safest location for a cable.

National jurisdictions do not stop at the low tide mark of a territory, they extend out into the sea and the seafloor. The 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (PDF) defined sovereign territorial waters as a 12-mile zone extending out from an economy’s coast. Every coastal economy has exclusive rights to the oil, gas, and other resources in the seabed up to 200 nautical miles from shore or to the outer edge of the continental margin, whichever is the further, subject to an overall limit of 350 nautical miles (650km) from the coast or 100 nautical miles (185km) beyond the 2,500-metre isobath (a line connecting equal points of water depth).

What does this mean for submarine cables? From the point where the cable enters territorial waters, any physical activity related to the cable requires the permission of the authorities. All cable construction and repair operations carried out in these sovereign areas also require the permission of the economy that has exclusive rights to the sea and seafloor.

Location and repair

Locating a cable break is straightforward. An optical pulse will be reflected at the point of a cable break, which can provide the distance to the fault from the start of the cable with considerable precision. At that point, it becomes a marine operation.

A specialist cable repair ship must be engaged, which, in turn, must obtain the relevant government’s permission to work at the location of the cable fault (don’t forget that only 2% of outages occur in international waters). Once at the break location, the repair vessel drags a grapnel along the seabed to hook the cable, cuts it, recovers one end, buoys it off, then recovers the other end. A new section is spliced into the cable aboard the ship in a jointing cabin, the fibre fusion-spliced and tested, the joint rebuilt and sealed against pressure, and the repaired cable laid back down with enough slack to reach the seabed.

The cost of a repair can vary greatly, depending on the location and depth of the fault, the nature of the contracted arrangements for cable repair, the amount of time the cable operator is willing to wait for a repair vessel and crew, and the weather. USD 500k to USD 1M is a representative cost of a single cable repair.

While the number of cables has grown, the time taken to obtain permission to operate repairs in territorial waters has generally increased. Industry data indicates repair response times have more than doubled over the past decade, and the longest single repair recorded in 2023 took 947 days, many of which were spent waiting for permission to undertake the repair.

There is also the issue of repair vessels. The industry has roughly 60 ships capable of repairing a submarine cable, operated under maintenance agreements that pool the cost of running this fleet across cable owners in each geographic region. These collective Submarine Cable Maintenance and Repair Agreements are used in the Atlantic Ocean, the North American Western Coastal region, the Mediterranean, South East Asia and the Indian Ocean, and Yokohama in the North Pacific (Figure 7).

Analysis by TeleGeography and Infra-Analytics has found that around two-thirds of cable maintenance vessels will reach the end of their service lives by 2040, while total cable kilometres are projected to grow by about 48% over the same period. Closing that gap would take USD 3B and require fifteen replacement ships plus five additional vessels simply to hold current service levels as the submarine cable network expands. The immediate problem is that nobody obviously owns this bill. Cable maintenance is funded through shared agreements that have been optimized for decades to be as cheap as possible, which worked when the fleet was young and is precisely the wrong structure for financing a fleet renewal.

This is the core of the cable resilience problem. Adding cable routes is comparatively easy, because today’s hyperscale cloud companies fund much of the new construction themselves and have strong commercial reasons to do so. However, no individual cable is so critical that it can sustain a business case to operate a dedicated repair fleet. The industry uses pooled resources, which suffer from under-investment.

Investigating cable outages

A rundown of recent cable outages includes:

Subsea cables were damaged in October 2023 by the anchor of the Hong Kong-flagged Newnew Polar Bear operating in the Baltic Sea.

Three cables in the Red Sea were cut in February 2024 by the drifting Rubymar vessel after it was struck by a missile.

The C-Lion1 and the BCS East-West Interlink cables were cut in the Baltic Sea in November 2024 with the Chinese bulk carrier Yi Peng 3 nearby.

Four cables were damaged in December 2024, with anchor drag marks on the Baltic seabed and the Cook Islands-registered tanker Eagle S detained.

Three major cables, including SEA-ME-WE 4 and IMEWE, were cut in the Red Sea in September 2025.

Finland and Estonia lost connections again in December 2025, with anchor drag confirmed by March 2026 on Baltic cables.

In August 2026, the Indigo West and Indigo Central cables off Perth were damaged, with a UAE-managed tanker under investigation by Australian Federal Police.

The outcomes are much less uniform than this list suggests. Swedish authorities found no conclusive evidence of wrongdoing in the Yi Peng 3 case and ruled the January 2025 Latvia-to-Gotland damage accidental. A Finnish court dismissed the case against the Eagle S captain in October 2025. United States and European officials concluded that several of the Baltic incidents were accidental. The captain of the Hong Tai 58 was convicted in Taiwan and sentenced to three years over the Taiwan to Penghu No. 3 cable, and the Newnew Polar Bear captain faced criminal damage charges in Hong Kong. The April 2026 Matsu fault turned out to have been caused by the wreck of a stranded fishing boat shifting onto the cable.

Anchor dragging is a common occurrence, particularly among poorly maintained merchant vessels in bad weather, accounting for a large share of ordinary faults every year. This may explain why investigators keep reaching inconclusive findings in good faith.

Who is responsible for cable resilience?

Cable systems have changed in recent decades.

The old telephone system regarded each cable as a self-contained system. The cable owner was responsible for its own resilience, independent of any other cables that may exist on similar routes. The telephone’s data carriage system typically used a ring architecture, where any outage in the ring caused the traffic to flow along the other half of the ring. If the ring used diverse paths, then any individual outage in the ring could be repaired immediately.

However, the implication of this design was that the actual capacity of the system was double the usable capacity. The cost of using such a cable reflected this 50% carriage efficiency.

In their search for cheaper services, Internet Service Providers (ISPs) wanted to purchase non-backed-up cable capacity, at a price that reflected this greater efficiency of cable use. They purchased this cheaper form of cable capacity on multiple cable systems. Individual outages caused a break in that cable’s service, but the ISP could reroute their traffic to use capacity that had been purchased on other cable systems which were not affected by the outage. For Internet traffic, this failover function is readily achieved in the routing system.

The overall outcome was that the responsibility for resilience shifted from the individual cable operator to the network operator. Cable outages would still cause a drop in available capacity. But as most Internet traffic is elastic, the drop in capacity would cause a drop in performance but not cause a complete shutdown.

Resilience and critical infrastructure considerations

Submarine cable systems are built by private consortia, repaired by private contracts that collectively fund a commercial repair fleet, regulated by coastal states individually, and governed internationally by international conventions drafted long before the Internet existed.

It would be good if permissions to repair submarine cables were granted in a streamlined manner so that repairs were not stalled for months awaiting a government’s approval to operate in their waters. It would be even better if emergency procedures were agreed in advance rather than negotiated during an outage.

Collectively, the industry needs to invest in repair capacity to upgrade an ageing repair fleet. Who undertakes this investment and how the repair capability is managed as a common asset is proving to be a difficult issue. In the worst case, it will be back to every cable for itself, and the inevitable outcome of higher costs and potentially slower repairs.

Geographic choke points will persist, geology will not stop, extreme weather and changing sediment conditions will continue to pose a threat to these cables. Route diversity is an effective response to these challenges, but economic clustering works against cable route diversity. Each cable would like to run through the shortest and cheapest route, and no cable operator is specifically motivated to spend additional sums to take a diverse route to the other existing cables.

None of this is technologically difficult, but it can be institutionally and economically difficult, which is harder.

Looking forward

The telephone company consortium model that funded and operated almost all the world’s subsea cables 30 years ago has come to an end. The service life of the entire inventory of cables and service vessels that they operated is also coming to an end.

Approximately a quarter of the world’s current subsea cable kilometres are projected to be decommissioned and retired by 2030. This massive retirement of capacity amounts to 845,000 kilometres of subsea fibre-optic cables at the end-of-life cycle for submarine infrastructure laid during the massive Internet boom of the late 1990s and early 2000s. Specifically, TAT-8 and TAT-14 in the Atlantic Ocean are being decommissioned, SEA-ME-WE-3, linking Europe and Asia, has been retired, and Japan-US and China-US have ended operations. In addition, more than half of the current repair vessel fleet will have reached their retirement point by 2040.

In their place are cable projects that are either fully funded or partially funded by the current US digital giants. This raises sovereign risk eyebrows in many economies, where the only communications conduits for an economy are owned and operated by a foreign entity. It also raises the question of sovereign control over the submarine repair vessel fleet and the existing maintenance pooling arrangements through submarine cable maintenance zones.

By 2028, Google will own the largest set of cables, measured by kilometres, in the Pacific, Atlantic and Indian Oceans, and based on current plans it will have more than 50% of the entire cable inventory under its control in the Indo-Pacific region. Similar centralization scenarios are playing out in the Atlantic Ocean as well. At this point, the sovereign risk eyebrows should be hitting the ceiling, as such a dominant position gives this single company unilateral control over the maintenance arrangements and associated repair vessel operations for the entire world’s communications network.

This is a serious issue for us, both as individuals and societally as we try to preserve the integrity and utility of our common communications infrastructure. The stability and productivity of our societies rely on our ability to communicate with each other seamlessly, efficiently and privately.

Passing the investment and operational costs of the public telecommunications services from public to private hands in the latter part of the 20th century was seen as a smart move. The move used private finance to fund the reinvigoration of national telecommunications infrastructure as it shifted from time-based voice switching to a far larger packet switching architecture to support computer-mediated communications and service provision.

However, we may see more uncomfortable outcomes looming in the near future. It was thought that the discipline of competition would rein in the potential abuses by private operators of the privileged position of operating a public communications service. That is not what happened.

Not only are public telecommunications systems now largely in private hands, but we are also seeing consolidation of the global telecommunications system to a few private entities, with no competition. Their accountability is not to the public or users of the service. Their accountability is to their institutional investors to continually improve their value and profitability. Nothing else.

So where does this leave the submarine cable system and efforts to maintain its critical function with the appropriate levels of resilience that reflect their critical role in global communications? Outside the US, few individual economies, if any, have the resources to meaningfully respond to this challenge. The European Union (EU) has taken some action to contribute to funding a fleet of repair vessels and taken measures to improve surveillance on submarine cables as a matter of regional security, but no other economies appear to be following this lead. It would certainly be ironic if this EU money were to end up simply funding the maintenance of Google’s submarine cable assets!

Back to the topic of cable resilience, viewed at a global level: Communications resilience is largely an ocean infrastructure question. Answers to this question rely on:

Detailed and current seabed surveys

Shipping controls to prevent anchoring and seabed fishing in declared subsea cable protection zones

A distributed repair fleet and crews trained to perform repair tasks

Rapid clearance to operate in territorial waters

Some coordination of action is necessary to open diverse cable routes and avoid single points of vulnerability and potential failure. The global cloud, for all its connotations of weightless air, firmly rests on the solidity of the seabed, and it can be no more reliable than conventions that we collectively adopt to look after it.

The Matsu Islands are an archipelago of 36 islands in the East China Sea, alongside the southeastern coast of mainland China. The islands have been administered since 1949 by Taiwan, part of a larger set of outlying islands administered by Taiwan, which includes the Kinmen and Penghu Islands, which all lie in the Taiwan Strait.

The Matsu Islands are connected to Taiwan’s main island by two submarine cables — Taima No.2, Taima No.3, and soon Taima No.4. The Taiwan Strait is a shallow body of water, with an average depth of 70m. The submarine cables that lie on this seafloor are vulnerable to damage from ship-based activity, like being snagged by fishing equipment or anchors. But these particular cables have been remarkably unlucky. Between 2018 and 2022, the submarine cables between Taiwan and the Matsu Islands were cut 27 times, and there have been four major outages in the three years from 2023 to 2025.

That’s not the only location where submarine cables have suffered many faults. The Baltic Sea is a shallow sea that has a dozen or so submarine communications cables, and undersea electricity and gas pipelines. There have been 11 disruptions to these submarine systems since 2023. Again, a very unlucky track record.

There are an estimated total of 1.5M kilometres of subsea communications cables, used by 607 in-service submarine cable systems (Figure 1) that are critical to the world’s telecommunications services. If they are put out of service for any reason, our satellite systems simply could not replace them. In such a catastrophic scenario, some communities would be totally isolated, with severe logistical and economic ramifications.
https://blog.apnic.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-14-at-11.57.54-am-1024x537.png
blocks.c: Figure 1 — Submarine cables, October 2026. Source: Telegeography.

blocks.x: We regard this collection of submarine cable systems as critical infrastructure for global communication services, and we take care to make them as resilient as possible. Modern warfare can deliberately disrupt communications systems, which adds another source of potential damage to the list of geological and accidental risks facing subsea cables.

On the night of 4 August 1914, days after Britain declared war against Germany, the British cable ship HMTS Alert sailed from Dover into the English Channel. The vessel dragged grappling hooks along the seabed, hauled up five German transatlantic and European telegraph cables, and cut them. This severed Germany’s direct, secure submarine cable links to the Americas, Africa, Spain, and the rest of Europe. Germany was forced to rely on wireless radio transmissions, where British intelligence could readily eavesdrop. If the German cryptography used to protect these wireless communications was broken, then it allowed the British to track military movements and capture critical messages, such as the Zimmermann Telegram.
This same action to deliberately sever undersea cables was repeated by the British in September 1939, cutting German cables to Lisbon and New York.
Protecting the cable
These thin polyester-coated cables at the bottom of the ocean are vulnerable, including to:
Geology in the form of submarine earthquakes or landslips
Being snagged by dragging ship anchors or fishing equipment along the seafloor
Deliberate attacks on the cables with grapnels and cutting equipment

How can cables defend against such risks? The inner core of the fibre optic cables and its copper conductor sheath can be wrapped in additional layers of steel cable jacketing as a form of armour (Figure 2). This is mostly used to reduce its vulnerability to shipping accidents.
https://blog.apnic.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-14-at-11.58.57-am-1-edited.png
blocks.c: Figure 2 — Cross-section of a submarine cable. Source: Telegeography.

blocks.x: Figure 2 is somewhat misleading. What is depicted here is a cross-section of submarine cable used in the segments of the cable that lead to the surface cable station. The cable segments that are laid on the deep-sea floor use just the inner components: Optical fibre and a single thin steel thread wrapped in a silicone gel, surrounded by a copper sheath (used to power the cable repeaters), and wrapped in polyethylene. There are no external armour elements. These deep-sea cable segments are around 20mm in diameter, or the size of a garden hose.

The cable surfaces at a cable landing station. These landing stations are typically plain, secured facilities with reliable power. The preferred location is a coastal point with a low volume of fishing or other maritime traffic, and a steep rise from the deep-sea floor. Cables are at their greatest risk from coastal shipping activity, so the shorter the distance from the deep-sea floor to the cable station on dry land, the better.
https://blog.apnic.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/subsea-landing.jpg
blocks.c: Figure 3 — Cable landing station. Source: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 3.0.

blocks.x: Many jurisdictions also declare ‘Cable Protection Zones’ as a warning to marine vessel operators that there are cables on the seafloor in this area, and ships should refrain from fishing activity and anchoring in these areas.
Cable routing
Cable routing is also important in terms of resilience. There are several objectives in a cable route, and not all of them can be optimized at the same time.
The cable route should be as short as possible, as additional cable length raises capital costs and increases end-to-end signal delay.

Cables should avoid areas of active geological activity where possible, such as tectonic plate boundaries and mid-plate rifts. Deeper is better, but within reason. Cables on the floor of a deep ocean section are less vulnerable to shipping activity and hostile efforts to disrupt the cable, but with extreme depths it’s more challenging to locate and raise the cable when undertaking a repair.

Sometimes there are geographic ‘choke points’ through which many cables are routed. Houthi-controlled waters remain effectively ungovernable for cable protection.
https://blog.apnic.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-14-at-12.01.41-pm-1024x465.png
blocks.c: Figure 4 — Cable routes in the Bab al-Mandab Strait.

blocks.x: There is also the Singapore Strait, a major junction for 35 cable systems (Figure 5). This is a shallow water strait that also hosts a significant volume of surface shipping.
https://blog.apnic.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-14-at-12.02.30-pm.png
blocks.c: Figure 5 — Cable routes in the Singapore Strait.

blocks.x: Further north, between Taiwan and the Philippines is the Luzon Strait, where 18 cables pass (Figure 6). This was the location of an earthquake and a subsequent set of submarine landslides in December 2006 that not only severed all the cables running through this strait, but also buried many of them under deep layers of sediment. It took 11 repair vessels 49 days to bring all the cable systems back into operation.
https://blog.apnic.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-14-at-12.03.24-pm-1024x759.png
blocks.c: Figure 6 — Cable routes in the Luzon Strait.

blocks.x: The Black Sea is an area with geopolitical risk and regulatory gaps. While mine risk is confirmed, no cable faults have been directly documented in the war in Ukraine. Russia’s continued presence and the conflict make this region functionally inaccessible for routine cable maintenance.

Geopolitics also plays a role in cable routing. Cable owners will prefer to avoid routes through politically unstable territorial waters if suitable alternative routes exist. There are also political considerations. If a cable lands in US territory, then the cable is subject to several Federal Communications Commission (FCC) constraints, including banning equipment or services from companies the FCC see as a threat to US national security. The FCC has also refused to permit the landing of a cable on US territory if the cable also lands in a territory that the US deems to be a foreign adversary.

Land routes are avoided in general, but there are some circumstances where a land route is the preferred option. Connectivity between Asia and Europe would normally run through the Bab al-Mandab Strait, landing in Egypt in the Gulf of Suez, then overland through Egypt to get to the Mediterranean Sea. There is an alternative route through the Persian Gulf, Iraq and Türkiye, although this entails a segment that transits the Strait of Hormuz, or a second overland segment through Oman and the United Arab Emirates.

So where does this leave the submarine cable system and efforts to maintain its critical function with the appropriate levels of resilience that reflect their critical role in global communications? Outside the US, few individual economies, if any, have the resources to meaningfully respond to this challenge. The European Union (EU) has taken some action to contribute to funding a fleet of repair vessels and taken measures to improve surveillance on submarine cables as a matter of regional security, but no other economies appear to be following this lead. It would certainly be ironic if this EU money were to end up simply funding the maintenance of Google’s submarine cable assets!
Back to the topic of cable resilience, viewed at a global level: Communications resilience is largely an ocean infrastructure question. Answers to this question rely on:
Detailed and current seabed surveys
Shipping controls to prevent anchoring and seabed fishing in declared subsea cable protection zones
A distributed repair fleet and crews trained to perform repair tasks
Rapid clearance to operate in territorial waters

Some coordination of action is necessary to open diverse cable routes and avoid single points of vulnerability and potential failure. The global cloud, for all its connotations of weightless air, firmly rests on the solidity of the seabed, and it can be no more reliable than conventions that we collectively adopt to look after it.
